# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **About 1.8 million people face emergency hunger in Yemen as strikes widen.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) Yemen strikes widen as hunger hits emergency levels
**What happened (neutral):** Yemen’s internationally recognised government has launched air strikes across Houthi-held territory, and Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili, a military spokesman, said government forces carried out 726 attacks in the 24 hours before Friday and claimed 121 fighters and commanders were killed or wounded, Al Jazeera reported. Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said the Saudi-led coalition that backs the government hit more than six governorates overnight, including a gas station in Sanaa’s Tahrir district that injured 13 people, three of them critically, and a later strike that the Houthis said killed a man and his wife in their home. He also described raids on a fuel station in Bani Matar, on Taiz, and five raids in Mocha that targeted a power station. Houthi-affiliated media reported that a Saudi air strike killed 11 civilians, most of them children, in al-Turbah in Taiz; Al Jazeera could not confirm that toll, and coalition forces did not comment. The government-run Saba news agency reported that Houthi attacks on government locations in Taiz on Saturday killed three civilians, including a 10-year-old boy, and wounded three others, including an infant. Coalition officials said a Houthi missile aimed at Riyadh was intercepted. The claims and casualties could not be independently verified. The World Food Programme and the Food and Agriculture Organization — the United Nations agencies for food aid and farming — warned on Friday that hunger in Yemen is likely to worsen over the next six months. About 1.8 million people faced emergency levels of hunger in government-held areas. More than 300,000 people have been newly displaced since the escalation began, mostly in Taiz, Lahij and Aden. The agencies said the Houthis encircled Taiz in early October, that Houthi-held areas were becoming harder to reach, and that the group was holding 73 United Nations staff. Aid groups say donor cuts, including by the United States and other Western countries, have deepened the crisis, with food and fuel prices soaring.

**Context & perspectives:** The Iran-backed Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, and Saudi Arabia led a coalition from March 2015 in support of the recognised government. Fighting resumed in July after a 2022 ceasefire collapsed, amid tensions around the United States-Israel war on Iran. Al-Nuzaili said fighting was ongoing in Ma’rib, al-Jawf, Taiz, Lahij, Shabwah, Midi and al-Dhale.

This is CONTESTED. The shared ground is that strikes and ground fighting have resumed and that the two United Nations food agencies, not either army, produced the hunger and displacement figures. Colonel al-Nuzaili’s case is that 726 attacks in a day are a military campaign against Houthi fighters and commanders, with 121 of them killed or wounded, and that Houthi fire — including a missile toward Riyadh and attacks that Saba said killed civilians in Taiz — is what government forces are answering. The Houthi account, carried by Houthi-affiliated media, is that a Saudi strike in al-Turbah killed 11 civilians, most of them children, so the offensive is landing on families, not only on fighters. Al Jazeera could not confirm that civilian toll, the coalition did not comment, and neither side’s casualty claims were independently verified — a limit each account has to live with.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/yemen-governmen-forces-hit-houthi-positions-as-un-warns-of-hunger-crisis?traffic_source=rss) — strikes, casualty claims, and the United Nations hunger warning

## Major world stories (3)
### 1) Spain votes Sunday on Sanchez’s record
**What happened (neutral):** Voters in Spain head to a snap election on Sunday that could bring the far-right Vox party into national government for the first time in five decades, half a century after Francisco Franco’s dictatorship ended, Al Jazeera reported. The campaign, which closed on Friday, turned on housing and immigration. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, 54, of the Socialist Workers’ Party, has been in power since 2018. Polls suggest the conservative People’s Party will win the most seats but will need Vox, projected third, to reach the 176 seats required for a majority in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies. Most surveys put the two together at that number, which would give People’s Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo a coalition or a minority government backed by Vox. Sanchez called the vote in October after parliament rejected two measures meant to protect renters, following protests over housing costs and evictions. The European Commission forecasts growth of 2.6 percent for Spain this year, against 1.2 percent for the eurozone. France 24 reported that Vox built its campaign on immigration after tens of thousands of people crossed into Ceuta, a Spanish city in North Africa, from Morocco in July. The South China Morning Post noted that Europe is opening an electoral cycle over the next 12 months that could shift the balance inside the European Union.

**Context & perspectives:** Alvaro Sanchez-Garcia, a political scientist at Spain’s Centre for Political and Constitutional Studies, told Al Jazeera the vote has been framed as a yes or no on Sanchez, and that switchers mostly stay inside the same left or right bloc. In 2023 Sanchez’s party finished second and he stayed in office with support from parties to his left and from Catalan and Basque groupings. Sanchez has clashed with United States President Donald Trump, refused a request from other NATO members — the North Atlantic Treaty Organization — to lift defence spending to 5 percent, and called Israel’s war in Gaza a genocide. On Friday he told a radio interviewer, “I can’t conceive of us losing,” and told a Madrid rally, “This election about one thing only: Whether Spain moves forward or goes backwards.”

This is CONTESTED. Sanchez’s case, in his own framing, is that Spain has never been in better shape: faster growth than a stagnant eurozone, and a progressive record that has made him a reference point for the European left. The limit his own allies cannot wish away is the October defeat of the renter measures that forced this vote. Feijoo’s case, put to Sanchez in a televised debate last week, is that national income is not a meal — “You can’t eat GDP” — and that alleged corruption and opportunism require a change of government. Isabel Labayen, 64, a longtime People’s Party voter, asked how Spain can be praised abroad when people cannot afford a house or food, or see a doctor in days rather than months. Vox’s case, as France 24 described the campaign, is that the July arrivals in Ceuta made immigration the issue that should decide the government. Polls are not ballots, and Feijoo still needs Vox for 176 seats.

**Questions to consider:** Do the People’s Party and Vox together reach 176 seats when Sunday’s count is finished?

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/two-visions-of-spain-collide-as-voters-weigh-sanchez-record?traffic_source=rss) — polls, the housing trigger, and the campaign’s closing arguments
- [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/news/world/europe/article/3376131/spains-pm-sanchez-makes-final-bid-head-conservatives-and-far-right) — Friday’s final appeal and the wider European election calendar
- [France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/immigration-a-key-issue-in-sunday-s-spanish-snap-election) — Vox’s focus on the July arrivals in Ceuta
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/28/world/europe/spain-pedro-sanchez-conservatives-election.html) — Sanchez as a Trump critic facing a right-wing challenge
- [Al Jazeera video](https://www.aljazeera.com/video/newsfeed/2026/11/28/spain-faces-political-shift-as-far-right-gains-ground?traffic_source=rss) — the possibility of Vox entering government

### 2) Trump backs Baghdad’s push on oil routes and borders
**What happened (neutral):** United States President Donald Trump on Friday endorsed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s campaign against oil smuggling, Al Jazeera reported. In a Truth Social post he wrote that Washington supports efforts “to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state,” and to build an Iraq that “makes its own political decisions.” It was Washington’s first comment on the tension between Baghdad and Erbil, the seat of the semi-autonomous Kurdish region. On Tuesday al-Zaidi moved to put the region’s border crossings and several oilfields under federal control. On Wednesday Iraq’s top court ruled that Baghdad may deploy federal forces along all international borders, including the Kurdish region’s. On Thursday Iraq closed two crossings there, one with Syria and one with Iran. Talks between Baghdad and Erbil are due on December 1, sponsored by the head of Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council.

**Context & perspectives:** The crackdown started in Jurf al-Sakhar, also called Jurf al-Nasr, in Babil province south of Baghdad. Kataib Hezbollah, an Iran-backed armed group the United States designates a terrorist organisation, has held the town since 2014, when it and allied groups took it from ISIL, the Islamic State, and most Sunni residents were displaced. Senior Iraqi security and oil officials told Reuters that the group has run an oil-smuggling network there, siphoning state crude worth hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021. Nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed and referred to the courts. Kataib Hezbollah denies the allegations. Al-Zaidi gave the group until November 20 to leave. A day before the deadline, after reported intervention by Esmail Qaani, head of Iran’s Quds Force, government forces entered and set up a joint operations centre; Kataib Hezbollah units are due to withdraw gradually as army, federal police, energy police and Popular Mobilisation Forces units deploy in phases. Harakat al-Nujaba and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada have also refused to disarm. After armed groups missed a September 30 deadline to hand over weapons, the government pushed that deadline to June 2027. Government spokesperson Haider al-Aboudi told the Iraqi News Agency that Iraq lost an estimated $100 billion between 2008 and 2025 from oil smuggled through the Kurdish region. Salim Zakhour, a constitutional-law researcher, told Al Jazeera the American post tells Kurdish leaders that Baghdad’s measures have strong American backing.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/why-is-trump-backing-iraqs-anti-smuggling-campaign?traffic_source=rss) — Trump’s post, the court ruling, and the smuggling allegations

### 3) El Nino floods hit Piura and add to Ecuador’s toll
**What happened (neutral):** Cities in Peru and Ecuador are flooding after downpours linked to an exceptionally strong El Nino — a warming of the sea surface in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific that shifts wind and rain worldwide — Al Jazeera reported. In Piura, northern Peru, waist-high water filled streets after 12 hours of heavy rain that began on Thursday. Luis Vasquez, chief of the National Institute of Civil Defence, told RPP radio that preliminary reports put the number of affected families in Piura at about 2,000. Floodwater forced the Jose Cayetano Heredia Hospital to move patients from its respiratory-infection ward to the auditorium, and more serious patients to intensive care. The Plaza de Armas and many businesses and public buildings were also hit. Peru’s armed forces have sent personnel and pumps; some residents said machines stopped for lack of fuel. The national weather service warned that moderate to heavy rain could continue in parts of the region for four days. President Keiko Fujimori postponed a trip to Colombia and said she plans to travel to the affected areas. The navy blamed El Nino for ocean swells that damaged Pacific-coast infrastructure and temporarily closed dozens of ports. In Ecuador, the National Secretariat for Risk Management said on Friday that 34 people had died and 47,000 had been affected. In Manta, two rivers broke their banks; resident Fernanda Navarrete said she had been “soaking in mud for four days” and had lost furniture, clothes and appliances. Peru and Ecuador are among several Latin American countries that have declared national emergencies. This year’s El Nino is projected to be the strongest on record.

**Context & perspectives:** Resident Pierre Garavito, whose refrigerator was floating in his Santa Margarita home, told reporters this was only the first heavy rain of the episode and that he had lost everything. The South China Morning Post carried the same Piura toll from Vasquez and the same picture of waist-high water after Thursday’s rain.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/el-nino-linked-deluges-flood-cities-in-peru-ecuador?traffic_source=rss) — Piura, the Ecuador toll, and the El Nino link
- [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/news/world/americas/article/3376127/peru-ecuador-hit-el-nino-linked-floods) — the Piura flooding and the civil-defence figure

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 1) Uganda opens Africa’s first trial of an mRNA Ebola shot for children
**What happened (neutral):** Africa’s first clinical trial of an mRNA vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola has begun in Uganda, aimed at the strain behind the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Al Jazeera reported. The state-run Uganda Virus Research Institute said on Friday that the trial is with Moderna, the United States company that makes the vaccine. It is the second trial of the shot. Moderna’s first human trial began in Canada in August and enrolled adults aged 18 to 65. The Ugandan trial is the first to test safety and immune response in children aged 1 and above, and aims to enrol 224 volunteers. Richard Hatchett, chief executive of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, which is helping fund the vaccine, said children are often hit hardest when Ebola strikes and are too often last to get new vaccines. A second candidate, the ChAdOx1 vaccine from India’s Serum Institute and the University of Oxford, is due to begin testing in the Democratic Republic of the Congo on Monday. Gavi, the alliance that helps lower-income countries buy vaccines, signed a purchase commitment last week with the Serum Institute for 1.5 million doses and plans to have hundreds of thousands ready if trials succeed and the World Health Organization and the Congolese government approve them. Emanuele Capobianco, Gavi’s director of global health security, said he hoped those trials would finish in early 2027 and that the deal could bring deployment forward by months. On Thursday, Congolese government data showed at least 12,021 confirmed Ebola infections and 5,904 deaths since the outbreak began in mid-May. Uganda declared its own outbreak over on July 28, after 20 infections and two deaths, the Ministry of Health said.

**Context & perspectives:** The Ugandan trial does not replace the Congolese outbreak response. It asks whether this shot is safe and whether it prompts an immune response, including in children, before any wider use.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/uganda-starts-mrna-ebola-vaccine-trial-in-first-for-africa?traffic_source=rss) — the trial design, the purchase deal, and the outbreak toll

### 2) Indian workers in Germany rise sevenfold, and many jobs stay empty
**What happened (neutral):** The number of Indian workers paying into Germany’s social-security system has grown sevenfold in a decade, to more than 140,000, Deutsche Welle reported, many of them in information technology and health care. Pratyay Saikia, 25, from Haryana, answered a 2022 advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruiter placing Indian workers in checked jobs abroad. He arrived in Baden-Württemberg with 180 other Indians for apprenticeships, finished a three-year apprenticeship at Metzgerei Lederer, a butcher’s shop, and now works there full time. A 2024 Bertelsmann Foundation study concluded Germany needs 288,000 foreign skilled workers a year until 2040 to replace retirees. FMC Group, a consultancy, noted that more than 369,000 skilled jobs went unfilled in 2025. Germany is also seeking electricians, mechatronics technicians, solar-panel installers and truck drivers, not only nurses and software specialists.

**Context & perspectives:** Daniel Raja, managing director of NM NextMittelstand, a Düsseldorf recruiter linking German firms with Indian workers, said hiring an electrician from India is still new for many Mittelstand firms — the small and medium-sized companies — so they hesitate, and that workers’ councils sometimes resist because they believe “cheap Indian labor” will take jobs or cut wages. David Kipp, of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, said he is sceptical of lowering language requirements, because people with little German have less contact with German institutions and are easier to exploit. Saikia had reached B1, an intermediate level, and still found the theory classes hard until co-workers helped and his German improved.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/indian-workers-fill-germany-s-labor-gaps-but-face-hurdles-and-risks/a-80072882?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — the sevenfold rise, the vacancy studies, and the hiring hurdles

## Progress watch (1)
### 1) Mining explosives kill students beside a Kunar school
**What happened (neutral):** An explosion on Saturday near a middle school in Asadabad, in Afghanistan’s eastern Kunar province, killed students and injured scores more. Deutsche Welle, citing the Interior Ministry, reported at least seven students killed and nearly 100 injured. The ministry’s spokesperson said early reports point to negligent storage of explosives at a mining-company depot in the Andir Sir area, beside the school. Provincial police spokesman Farid Dehqan said the blast was around 10 a.m. Samiulhaq Haqbayan, the provincial information director, told the German press agency DPA that the explosives were for mining and for clearing hazardous rocks along the Kunar-Nuristan highway. No one has said what ignited them. The ministry said an investigation is ongoing. Al Jazeera quoted Mawla Dad, head of Kunar Provincial Hospital, who put the toll at at least six students killed and 97 injured, and said those figures were preliminary and could change. Mawlawi Sami-ul-Haq, Kunar’s director of information and culture, told Al Jazeera the blast was in a house beside a middle school in Andar Ser, used by people in mining who had stored dynamite there. Interior Ministry spokesman Mufti Abdul Mateen Qani said initial investigations point to negligence. Investigative teams were at the scene. It was the third explosion near a school or religious school in a week. Two blasts near religious schools in Kapisa and Farah killed five students in total; local officials blamed unexploded ordnance from earlier wars.

**Context & perspectives:** The two outlets differ on the first count: the Interior Ministry figure carried by Deutsche Welle is seven dead and nearly 100 injured; the hospital chief’s figure carried by Al Jazeera is six dead and 97 injured, and he said it could change. Both trace the blast to mining explosives stored beside the school, not to an attack. Mining is a major industry in a country rich in iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, gold, coal and gemstones, and safety standards at mining sites are often poor. Gemstone mining is growing in Kunar.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/afghanistan-several-killed-in-blast-near-middle-school/a-80084227?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — the ministry toll and the week’s earlier school blasts
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/students-killed-injured-in-school-explosion-in-afghanistans-kunar-region?traffic_source=rss) — the hospital’s preliminary count and the dynamite account

## Understanding the Issue: Why the party in first place can still miss the government
A common misreading of a European election night is that the party with the most seats has won the government. That is not how this kind of parliament works. The following is the host’s own explanation of the mechanism, not a finding from a separate study. A prime minister who loses a vote he or she treated as essential can dissolve the chamber and pick an early date, which is what a snap election is: the calendar moves, the rules for forming a government do not. In a multiparty chamber, governing requires a majority of seats, or enough partners to supply one, not a plurality. A first-place party that is short of that line must bargain with a rival whose voters it spent the campaign opposing, or stay in opposition while a second-place leader assembles a wider set of partners. Regional and nationalist parties can matter as much as the national runner-up, because their seats count the same on the night a government is proposed. Campaigns that sort voters into two blocs make that arithmetic starker: few people cross the aisle, so the result is less a swing of individuals than a test of which bloc can hold its own voters and then find allies. Abroad, a leader can be admired for foreign-policy stands that never appear on the domestic ballot, where rent, food and a doctor’s appointment decide the vote. When you next read a “winner” headline from a parliament like Spain’s, check whether any combination of named parties can actually seat a government — not only who finished first.

## Media-literacy note
Casualty claims in a war, and the first hours after a blast, often arrive from one side’s spokesman or one hospital, and they move. When two outlets give two tolls, keep both and note who counted. A poll is a survey of voters before they vote, not the seat total. For the stories that will still matter next week, open a second outlet from another country and look for the document underneath: a court ruling, a United Nations food analysis, a company or ministry statement.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **One million orbital computers won U.S. approval, moving heavy data work off Earth.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) U.S. clears a million orbital computers
**What happened (neutral):** The U.S. Federal Communications Commission, the agency that licenses radio uses including satellites, has authorised SpaceX to deploy one million orbital computing modules under a plan named Starmind, Al Jazeera reports. Chairman Brendan Carr said the approval lets SpaceX “deploy 1,000,000 orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth,” and called it a first in the country’s history. He said that under President Donald Trump the United States was moving so this technology “creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers benefits for the American people.”

**Context & perspectives:** SpaceX says the satellites would run artificial intelligence, software that finds patterns in huge data sets, in a low-latency sun-synchronous orbit and beam the results back, using the sun for power. The company calls that the fastest way to scale because electrical power on Earth is getting harder to find, and describes the plan as low-cost and high performance. Under the licence, deployment must begin no later than November 2033; 100,000 modules, 10 percent of the maximum, no later than November 2035; half by November 2038; and the full constellation by 2040. SatFleet Live, which tracks satellites in real time, counts 16,928 active satellites now, of which 11,190, or 66 percent, are SpaceX Starlink internet satellites. Data centres on the ground need land, water and power and throw off heat. An article the Environmental and Energy Study Institute, a U.S. nonprofit, published in 2025 said large data centres can use up to 5 million gallons of water a day, about the use of a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. Those pressures have brought protests in the United States, Kenya and India. In July, opponents of rapid data-centre growth held 142 protests across 42 U.S. states, and Al Jazeera says polling data showed opposition was a key issue for many voters in this month’s U.S. midterm elections.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/27/why-does-elon-musk-want-to-put-a-million-satellite-data-centres-in-space?traffic_source=rss) — FCC authorisation, licence dates, and the water and protest figures

## Major world stories (3)
### 2) New Zealand’s final count leaves a new centrist party with the deciding seats
**What happened (neutral):** Final results of New Zealand’s November 7 election, released Friday, leave Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s centre-right coalition one seat short of a majority, Al Jazeera reports. Luxon’s National Party and its partners, populist New Zealand First and libertarian ACT, won 65 seats: National 40, ACT 13, New Zealand First 12. Parliament has 130 members, so 66 are needed. Labour, the largest opposition party, won 36. Qiulae Wong’s new centrist Opportunity Party won 7 seats.

**Context & perspectives:** Al Jazeera ties the shortfall to lost support in a stagnant economy. Luxon has been prime minister since 2023. The Associated Press likewise reports a deadlocked final result with the centrist newcomer as the decider. If no agreement is reached, voters could return to the polls next year. Luke Oldfield, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, told Reuters a deal was likely and that a right-hand bloc was highly likely, not a second election.

**Contested:** The count both camps have to live with is 65 seats against a 66-seat majority, with Wong’s 7 the only ready bridge. Luxon told a news conference that New Zealanders need a government that is stable, works together and will last the full term — the case for adding one partner rather than sending the country back to the polls. Wong has promised a universal basic income of up to 370 New Zealand dollars, about 208 U.S. dollars, a week, more action on climate change, a ban on bottom-trawling fishing, healthcare reforms, and a kinder style of politics, and she has pledged to do everything she can to ensure a stable government. That package is the price of her seats. It collides with partners Luxon already has. Winston Peters of New Zealand First promises tighter immigration and withdrawal from the Paris Climate Accord, the global climate treaty; he has called opponents “morons” and told a Chinese-born lawmaker to “go back to your country.” Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour of ACT campaigned against a greater governance role for the Indigenous Maori minority and promised large cuts to state spending. Wong’s own pledge of stability does not erase that clash, and Luxon’s case for a lasting government still depends on a partner those two may not accept. Oldfield’s reading is that a right-hand deal is still the likely end.

**Questions to consider:** Will Luxon name a governing partner, or will the alternative of a fresh election next year become the path?

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/27/new-zealand-election-results-set-up-tricky-talks-for-conservative-incumbent?traffic_source=rss) — seat totals, Wong’s programme, and Oldfield’s reading
- [AP News](https://apnews.com/article/new-zealand-election-results-a19a838d8256a0762703ff0572aca3e6) — final result leaves the centrist newcomer as decider

### 3) Cologne court orders the archdiocese to pay 550,000 euros
**What happened (neutral):** On Thursday the Higher Regional Court of Cologne ruled that the Archdiocese of Cologne must pay 550,000 euros, about 603,341 dollars, to a woman now 60, Deutsche Welle reports. Melanie F. was subjected to serious sexual abuse by a priest in the late 1970s and early 1980s. She had already received 360,000 euros, so the court added 190,000 euros. Before this, the highest court award in a similar case was 300,000 euros, granted by the Regional Court of Cologne in June 2023.

**Context & perspectives:** The Seventh Civil Senate pointed to an abortion performed without the knowledge or consent of the plaintiff, then 15, as a reason for a substantial increase. She reportedly became pregnant twice during the abuse. Born in 1966, she lived in a Catholic orphanage in Bonn. Bernd U., then a theology student and volunteer, later an ordained priest, took her and a boy two years older to live with him. From 1979 he abused her in his residence at the parish and threatened to send her back to the orphanage. He became legal guardian of both children. Cardinal Joseph Höffner, then Archbishop of Cologne, approved that arrangement. The higher court held the archdiocese liable under official liability and overruled the 2023 regional ruling, which had said the abuse was not sufficiently linked to his role as a priest and had happened in his capacity as a caregiver. The higher court said he gained her trust in a pastoral role the judges called a “cover,” that he would likely not have become foster father so easily without the cover of a celibate priest, and that most of the abuse took place in the rectory. Deutsche Welle reports that the 2023 ruling met disbelief inside an archdiocese already in turmoil over how Cardinal Rainer Maria Woelki handled abuse cases, after decades of church teaching that a priest is a priest in all he does.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/historic-€550-000-ruling-german-court-holds-catholic-church-liable-for-priest-s-abuse/a-80071917?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — the award, the earlier 300,000-euro ceiling, and the liability reasoning

### 4) Costa Rica bars a U.N. rapporteur at the airport
**What happened (neutral):** Costa Rica barred Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, an independent expert named by the U.N. Human Rights Council who does not speak for the U.N. itself, Al Jazeera reports. She was halted and held on Thursday at Juan Santamaría International Airport. Omer Badilla, director-general of the immigration authority, said she was refused entry because she is the subject of an international alert over links to terrorist acts, and that police enforce the law when national security is at risk. He did not say which country issued the alert.

**Context & perspectives:** She was appointed in 2022 and was travelling to receive an honorary doctorate from the University of Costa Rica. She has faced pushback from Israel and the United States over her advocacy for Palestinians and her accusations that Israel has committed genocide and other war crimes. The United States imposed sanctions on her after she criticised Washington’s policy on Gaza. President Laura Fernandez, in office since May, is a close ally of President Trump and has pursued closer trade ties with Israel. Israel declared Albanese persona non grata in 2024.

**Contested:** Badilla’s account is that an international alert tying her to terrorist acts made entry a national-security refusal, and that Costa Rican police had to apply that rule. The strongest case for going further, as Israel’s ambassador to the U.N., Danny Danon, put it in praise of Costa Rica, is that someone who uses a U.N. mandate to spread propaganda, legitimise terrorist organisations, desecrate the memory of the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust, and vilify the United States and Israel should face consequences. Albanese called the detention a disgrace and appalling, wrote that “you see the face of the empire the day you touch a nerve,” and told Semanario Universidad that being on the U.S. sanctions list did not explain a stop in Costa Rica: “We are not in the United States. We are in Costa Rica,” and “Is Costa Rica a sovereign country?” She said the only country she knew she could not enter was Israel. Badilla never named the alert’s author, and Albanese did not dispute that she knew she was on the U.S. list.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/27/costa-rica-denies-entry-to-uns-albanese-over-links-to-terrorist?traffic_source=rss) — the airport refusal, Badilla’s alert claim, and Albanese’s and Danon’s responses

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 5) Eurozone inflation is back at a three-year high
**What happened (neutral):** Inflation in the eurozone, the group of countries that use the euro, has doubled from 2 percent in December 2025 to 4 percent in October 2026, its highest level in three years, as conflict in the Middle East disrupts oil and gas, Al Jazeera reports. Energy inflation rose to 21 percent in October, the highest since December 2022, when it was 25.5 percent in the first winter after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics office.

**Context & perspectives:** The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the eurozone, lists Lithuania at 6.1 percent, Bulgaria at 5.9 percent and Greece at 5.7 percent as the highest rates. Cyprus went from 0.1 percent at the end of last year to 5.4 percent, Italy from 1.2 to 5.6, Belgium from 2.2 to 5.2, and France from 0.7 to 3.7. Inflation eased in Slovakia, from 4.1 percent to 2.9 percent, and Al Jazeera also lists easier readings in Estonia (3.6 percent), Latvia (3.1), Austria (3.5) and Malta (2.3). Eurostat says a typical basket of food, housing, energy and transport now costs 69 percent more than in 2000, with about two-fifths of that increase in the past four years. In 2022 prices jumped by more than 8 percent in a single year. Prices in Hungary have more than tripled since 2000, so something that cost 100 euros then costs about 335 euros now, after a 17 percent surge in 2023 alone. In Athens, Giorgos, a 40-year-old journalist, said his pay rose from 800 euros to 1,100 euros over two years and he is still borrowing to get by. In London, Emma, 33, called nearly 10 pounds for a return Tube ride ridiculous. The Wall Street Journal adds a newer national reading: inflation in France and Spain fell more than expected in November as fuel prices declined, but remained too high for the European Central Bank, which is expected to raise its key rate for a third time since the war between the United States and Iran began.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/27/borrowing-to-make-ends-meet-the-rising-cost-of-living-in-europe?traffic_source=rss) — October eurozone and country inflation figures
- [Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/world/europe/french-inflation-slides-on-drop-in-fuel-prices-2bd7e78e?mod=rss_worldnews) — November fuel-price drop in France and Spain, and the expected rate rise

### 6) A Gaza survey finds more than one in eight young children stunted
**What happened (neutral):** A nutritional survey by UNICEF, the United Nations Children’s Fund, and its partners in accessible areas of the Gaza Strip between May 31 and June 15, 2026, found that 12.2 percent of children under five were stunted, Al Jazeera reports. Only 22.4 percent of children aged six to 23 months received a minimum acceptable diet. Seven-year-old Nabigha al-Zaqzouq is 99 centimetres tall and weighs 10 kilograms. Five-year-old Tala Zidan is 94 centimetres, about 15 to 16 centimetres shorter than the average for her age, and her father says her height has barely changed in two years.

**Context & perspectives:** Nutritionist Nada Abu al-Nada says average food availability was about 2,580 calories per person per day before the war and estimated average consumption has fallen to about 1,000. At Nasser Hospital, endocrinologist Hani Sayed Zuhair says growth-problem cases in a single clinic session have risen from about 15 to 20 before the war to between 30 and 40 now. Families describe bread and canned food, and meals from charitable community kitchens. Nabigha’s mother, Alia, said that after the ceasefire they are living under a suffocating blockade and asked that medicines and treatments be allowed in. Tahrir Zidan said he has not been able to buy even one kilogram of meat, a chicken, or a kilogram of fruit.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/11/27/will-i-get-taller-gazas-children-suffer-stunting-amid-war-blockade?traffic_source=rss) — the UNICEF survey, calorie estimate, and clinic counts

## Progress watch (1)
### 7) A Shandong city turns retired buses into cafes and keeps transit jobs
**What happened (neutral):** Zaozhuang, in eastern China’s Shandong province, has turned retired buses into mobile cafes and in doing so helped save the jobs of more than 200 transit workers who were facing layoffs, the South China Morning Post reports. In 2023 Liang Yu left her job as a station attendant with the city’s public transit group to become a barista, according to the Southern Metropolis Daily. A decommissioned bus, refitted as a mobile coffee shop, was the start of that work.

**Context & perspectives:** The complication is the reason the jobs were at risk: ride-hailing apps and electric bikes have been pulling riders off the old bus network, so the cafe conversion is a rescue inside a shrinking service, not a return of the old ridership.

- [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture/trending-china/article/3376059/chinese-city-turns-retired-buses-mobile-cafes-retraining-transit-workers-baristas) — the bus cafes and the jobs kept

**A former Chinese tax official calls a wealth tax unavoidable: South China Morning Post**

**Two Egyptian court cases test an independent newsroom: The New York Times**
The fate of journalist Lina Attalah and her outlet, Mada Masr, in two court cases is being treated as a test of whether Egypt’s independent press can survive. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/27/world/middleeast/egypt-journalist-trial-lina-attalah-mada-masr.html)

## Understanding the Issue: Why a change of party rarely rewrites Iran policy
A common misreading is that a new majority in Washington resets policy toward Iran the way a new board resets a company. The record Al Jazeera sets out is a sanctions machine built across parties. After the 1979 Islamic revolution, Democratic President Jimmy Carter began imposing sanctions once the U.S. embassy in Tehran was seized, eight months after the U.S.-backed monarch Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi was overthrown. Democratic President Bill Clinton later widened that isolation with “dual containment” of Tehran and Saddam Hussein’s Iraq, and in 1996 signed sanctions on foreign companies investing in Iran’s energy sector; the bill passed the House of Representatives 415 to 0. After the September 11, 2001 attacks, Iran cooperated with the United States against the Taliban, and months later Republican President George W. Bush still placed Iran in an “axis of evil” with Iraq and North Korea. Historian Golnar Nikpour told Al Jazeera that proclamation shocked both reformists in Tehran and U.S. military leaders who had been working with Iran. Law professor Maryam Jamshidi told Al Jazeera that, until Trump, the heaviest rounds of Iran sanctions came under Democratic presidents Clinton and Obama, and that both parties have treated post-revolutionary Iran as an enemy to constrain. Reading an energy-price story beside that record means a leader’s call to end a war is not, by itself, a forecast that Iranian oil and gas return to market. The concrete check is whether a new Congress records a vote that keeps, tightens, or actually lifts secondary sanctions of the 1996 kind, rather than a sentence about ending the fighting. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/27/democrats-want-to-end-trumps-iran-war-but-how-different-are-they?traffic_source=rss)

## Media-literacy note
When two outlets describe the same event, put their documents side by side and mark which sentence is a measurement, which is a named person’s claim, and which is the writer’s conclusion. A court judgment, a licence, and an election return are checkable in a way a headline adjective is not. If a figure has no comparison — a previous year, a legal threshold, a headcount — treat it as incomplete until you find one.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **Kenya's court stopped a 50-bed US Ebola site until the deal is disclosed.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) Kenya's High Court halts work at a US-backed Ebola quarantine site
**What happened (neutral):** Al Jazeera reports that Kenya's High Court ruled on Thursday that the government breached the constitution by allowing a United States-backed Ebola quarantine site at a military airbase without disclosing the deal or seeking public comment. Judge Patricia Nyaundi ordered any further work stopped until those conditions are met. The 50-bed site sits inside Laikipia airbase near Nanyuki, in central Kenya, and was meant to quarantine people exposed to Ebola, including US citizens. Seven American aid workers who had been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo quarantined there in July. In June, Kenyan police opened fire on protesters against the site and at least one person was killed; the week before Thursday's ruling, hundreds marched in Nanyuki and at least two people were killed and one wounded. The same court had suspended construction in late May. It found that Health Minister Aden Duale had not obeyed that order; he later told the court he had ordered an immediate halt. Kenya's first imported case of the Bundibugyo Ebola strain — a form of the virus with no approved vaccine or treatment — was recorded in early October in a traveller from Congo via Uganda. As of mid-November the country had two deaths and seven other cases, all of whom recovered, and no new cases since October 19. The World Health Organization, the UN health agency, declared the outbreak an international public health emergency on May 17. The government has not commented on Thursday's ruling.

**Context & perspectives:** The dispute turns on whether a foreign health site on a military base can be built before the public sees the agreement. Residents of Nanyuki and Laikipia, in protests and in the case, say the United States is shifting Ebola risk onto Kenyans; their strongest reason is proximity — the beds are inside a Kenyan airbase, and people living beside it were not shown the deal. Kenyan and US authorities, before this ruling, publicly restated their commitment to the plan even after the May suspension; their reason is the outbreak itself — a quarantine for exposed people, including Americans who had worked in Congo, while Bundibugyo still has no approved vaccine. Nyaundi's ruling does not decide that medical question. It says residents were left "standing outside the sealed wooden window," able to tell that decisions were being made and denied a chance to know or take part. The court's own record also shows the May stop was not followed until Duale later said he had ordered work to cease.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/kenya-govt-violated-constitution-with-ebola-quarantine-site-court-says?traffic_source=rss) — High Court ruling, the Nanyuki site, protests, and Kenya's Bundibugyo cases

## Major world stories (3)
### 1) Two men arrested in Germany over an alleged synagogue plot
**What happened (neutral):** Deutsche Welle reports that Germany's federal prosecutor on Thursday ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens, identified as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., in Heidelberg and Cologne. Prosecutors say they are strongly suspected of membership in a domestic terrorist organization. More than 250 officers took part, and searches at 17 sites in three states were still going on. Prosecutors say Mostafa Al-R. was an associate of Mohammad Al-Saadi in the United States, accused of setting up a group called HAYI — Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya — which they say was responsible for attacks on US, Israeli, and Jewish institutions in Europe from March 2026, after the outbreak of Donald Trump's war with Iran. They say the two men founded a separate organization at the end of 2025 to prepare further attacks in Germany and Europe, gathered funds, and recruited people for explosive attacks. On two nights in late March 2026, prosecutors wrote, unknown assailants went — presumably with explosives — to synagogues in Cologne and in one other European city; the plan was not carried out, for reasons not yet known. The lead, prosecutors said, came from the BfV, Germany's domestic intelligence agency. The two were expected before judges later on Thursday for a decision on investigative detention. One other person is still being sought.

**Context & perspectives:** The prosecutor's account is the only detailed public case so far: a plot prepared, then not carried out, with the March approach to two synagogues as the clearest alleged act. The men have not had a quoted reply in this report. Deutsche Welle notes the story is still developing.

**Questions to consider:** Did judges later on Thursday order the two men held in investigative detention?

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/germany-2-arrested-suspected-of-plotting-synagogue-attack/a-80057715?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Arrests, the HAYI allegation, and the March approach to synagogues

### 2) Strikes in Gaza kill an education official and seven other people
**What happened (neutral):** Al Jazeera reports that Israeli attacks killed at least eight Palestinians across Gaza on Thursday, including Khaled Abu Nada, undersecretary of Gaza's Ministry of Education, and his wife, in an air strike in western Deir el-Balah. Medics at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital said six other people were wounded, several critically. Al Jazeera's Ashraf Abu Amra, reporting from Deir el-Balah, said Israeli Apache helicopters fired two missiles at a residential apartment during dawn prayers, in an area crowded with tents. In the north, a drone strike on a group in Gaza City's Shati refugee camp killed three and wounded four, al-Shifa Hospital said; a strike on Tuffah killed three; a drone attack on Nassr wounded several people. The deaths come during a ceasefire that took effect last October.

**Context & perspectives:** Everything turns on who Abu Nada was, and what killing him during a ceasefire is for. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz said the strike killed a Hamas figure responsible for the group's economy and education portfolios — their reason for the strike is that those portfolios are Hamas administration, not a civilian school office. Gaza's Ministry of Interior accuses Israel of trying to spread chaos by killing security and police commanders, after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, internal security chief for northern Gaza, was killed with his wife and two daughters early Wednesday, and Naim Abu Nahl, Gaza's internal security director, was killed the day before. Health Ministry spokesperson Zaher al-Wahidi told Al Jazeera that more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed, including 130 this month, and more than 6,000 wounded, in Israeli attacks since the ceasefire, and called it systematic targeting of "all the pillars of life." The ministry's overall toll since October 2023 is 74,746 killed. Neither statement concedes the other's description of Abu Nada.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/israeli-attacks-on-gaza-kill-senior-education-official-seven-other-people?traffic_source=rss) — Thursday's deaths, the Netanyahu-Katz statement, and ceasefire casualty figures

### 3) Explosion and fire shut a Bangkok oil refinery
**What happened (neutral):** Al Jazeera reports that an explosion and fire at Bangchak Corporation's Phra Khanong oil facility in eastern Bangkok injured at least seven people on Thursday, four of them seriously, according to the city's Erawan Emergency Medical Centre. The company said it shut all production units, contained the incident, and brought the situation under control. The Bangna District Office told people nearby to leave at once and said the cause was under investigation. A city alert said the fire was under control but told people to avoid the area. The site is described by the company as a refinery with a maximum capacity of 120,000 barrels a day. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said he was monitoring the situation, that it appeared under control, and that the fire did not seem to be in the main production area, without further detail. Al Jazeera's Tony Cheng reported the blast was heard at about 3 p.m. local time, that the site is near Bangkok's main port and supplies much of central Thailand's oil imports, and that the highway and most major routes there were still open.

**Context & perspectives:** An explosion at the same refinery in July 2012, then owned by Bangchak Petroleum, caused a large fire and no reported injuries. At the time, people asked why a plant of that size stood in what is now a residential part of the city. Cheng said industrial accidents have occurred in the area in the past couple of years. The extent of Thursday's damage is not yet known.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/explosion-occurs-at-oil-facility-in-thailands-bangkok?traffic_source=rss) — Injuries, shutdown, capacity, and the evacuation warning
- [AP News](https://apnews.com/article/thailand-bangkok-explosion-oil-facility-e8098146bfb994dffc14448b1027c5d1) — Bangkok authorities on a large explosion at a major oil facility

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 1) India and the United States reset the tariff argument
**What happened (neutral):** The Hindu reports that a new proposal from the USTR — the Office of the United States Trade Representative, which negotiates US trade deals — puts the tariff framework on India back to what it was when trade talks began. The same report says experts argue the tariffs are not a substantial threat and that India should not rush into a deal. Deutsche Welle reports that India has denied US claims that New Delhi's policies promote excess manufacturing capacity, and that India has told the United States to resolve tariff concerns in the talks. Reuters reports that President Donald Trump's new tariffs are aimed at prising global trade from China's grip.

**Context & perspectives:** New Delhi's case, as the government states it and as The Hindu's account of experts adds, is that this paper is a return to the opening bid, not a blow that forces a signature, and that the excess-capacity charge is wrong. Washington's case, as Reuters describes the tariff aim, is larger than the India text: use tariffs to pull trade away from China, so India's terms sit inside that contest rather than beside it. The articles do not record either government giving ground.

**Read more (sources):**
- [The Hindu](https://www.thehindu.com/business/Economy/experts-say-new-us-tariffs-do-not-pose-substantial-threat-india-should-not-rush-into-trade-deal/article71746007.ece) — USTR proposal and the argument against rushing a deal
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/india-news-resolve-tariff-concerns-in-trade-talks-india-tells-us/live-80056202?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — India's denial of the excess-capacity claim
- [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/trumps-new-tariffs-aim-prise-global-trade-chinas-grip-2026-11-26/) — Tariffs framed as a move to loosen China's hold on trade

### 2) Seabirds carry sensors toward fishing boats that switch tracking off
**What happened (neutral):** The New York Times reports that researchers are fitting seabirds with GPS — satellite location trackers — and audio gear to find fishing vessels that operate with no tracking signals, and to judge the environmental hazards those boats pose. A boat that turns its signal off is hard to see from satellites that read those signals; a bird that follows the boat can record where it went and what it sounded like.

**Context & perspectives:** The report is a methods story, not a count of boats found. It does not name a fleet, a fine, or a government response.

**Read more (sources):**
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/26/climate/seabirds-tracking-hidden-fishing-boats.html) — GPS and audio sensors on seabirds used to detect untracked vessels

## Progress watch (1)
### 1) War and drought squeeze Sudan's farms and water
**What happened (neutral):** Al Jazeera reports that attacks on electricity infrastructure and drought are threatening Sudan's harvests and leaving millions without water. The people most exposed are farmers whose livelihoods depend on that power and on rain that has not come.

**Context & perspectives:** The article presents both blows together: grid attacks from the war, and drought, hitting the same season. It does not name a relief shipment, a repair crew, or a ceasefire step for the power lines.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/11/26/war-and-drought-threaten-livelihoods-of-sudans-farmers?traffic_source=rss) — Harvests and water under attack and drought

### Also Today
**Ukraine drone attack kills five in Russian-occupied Zaporizhia: Al Jazeera**
A Russian-installed official said five people were killed and three wounded in Vesioloye, while Mayor Vitali Klitschko said ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv shopping centre and two other buildings. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/ukraine-drone-attack-kills-five-in-russian-occupied-zaporizhia?traffic_source=rss)

**DR Congo Ebola cases surpass 12,000 as fighting disrupts response in east: Al Jazeera**
Fighting in the east is displacing health workers and civilians as authorities try to contain the country's worst Ebola outbreak. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/dr-congo-ebola-cases-surpass-12000-as-fighting-disrupts-response-in-east?traffic_source=rss)

**Lured by High Salaries, Some Brazilians Were Duped Into Fighting for Russia: The New York Times**
Dozens of Brazilians were sent to the front with little training after recruiters promised pay that, the men say, never materialized. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/26/world/americas/brazil-recruiting-russia-army.html)

**Police use tear gas to disperse fresh Bangladesh garment worker protests: Reuters**
Police fired tear gas as garment workers protested again, after a wage rise that had not ended the dispute. Source: [reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/world-at-work/police-use-tear-gas-disperse-fresh-bangladesh-garment-worker-protests-2026-11-26/)

**Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling: BBC**
Myanmar is refusing to comply with parts of a ruling by the ICJ, the International Court of Justice, the United Nations' top court. Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c61wr87wyg5wo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Deadly factory fire in Indonesia renews lack of safety enforcement fears: South China Morning Post**
A Saturday blaze at the Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Cikande, Banten, killed 26 people, with about 30 still missing, and labour advocates warned that safety rules are not enforced consistently. Source: [scmp.com](https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/lifestyle-culture/article/3375934/deadly-factory-fire-indonesia-renews-lack-safety-enforcement-fears)

At least 13 miners died and others remain missing after heavy rain flooded an illegal gold mine in West Java. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/video/newsfeed/2026/11/26/rescuers-recover-bodies-after-flood-at-illegal-indonesia-gold-mine?traffic_source=rss)

US sanctions on the Canadian judge have left apps failing and bank transfers blocked, so the court is working around American firms. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/icc-judge-kimberly-prost-tries-war-crimes-shes-a-target-of-us-sanctions?traffic_source=rss)

**Indian court tightens food labelling proposal, asks global food firms to end 'double standards': Reuters**
An Indian court tightened a food-warning-label proposal and told global food companies to stop using double standards. Source: [reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/india/india-tightens-food-warning-labels-proposal-new-setback-industry-2026-11-26/)

**Malaysian air force facilities used to transport illicit drugs, minister says: Reuters**
A Malaysian minister said air force facilities had been used to move illicit drugs. Source: [reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/malaysian-air-force-facilities-used-transport-illicit-drugs-minister-says-2026-11-26/)

**Gaza meningitis cases surge as collapsing infrastructure fuels health fears: Al Jazeera**
Meningitis is spreading where overcrowding and damaged sanitation put children at higher risk. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/gaza-meningitis-cases-surge-as-collapsing-infrastructure-fuels-health-fears?traffic_source=rss)

**Photos: Rallies around the world denounce violence against women: Al Jazeera**
Rallies marked the day against a UN figure of about 47,000 women and girls intentionally killed by a partner or family member last year. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/11/26/photos-rallies-around-the-world-denounce-violence-against-women?traffic_source=rss)

**Hong Kong Grieves Fire Victims Under Watchful Eye of Authorities: The New York Times**
Residents quietly mourned 168 people killed in a high-rise blaze a year ago, while officials warned against using the disaster to sow division. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/26/world/asia/hong-kong-fire-wang-fuk-court-anniversary.html)

**Sri Lanka mass grave revives quest for answers to forgotten Muslim massacre: Al Jazeera**
A mass grave has renewed demands for answers about hundreds of Muslims killed while Tamil separatists fought the army. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/sri-lanka-mass-grave-revives-quest-for-answers-to-forgotten-muslim-massacre?traffic_source=rss)

**A Chinese consumer advocate is stranded in South Korea as a crackdown in China targets campaigners: AP News**
Consumer advocate Wang Hai is stranded in South Korea while a crackdown in China targets campaigners. Source: [apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/china-consumer-activist-wang-hai-south-korea-bbb712001f613da3b23edf383d390ae1)

**Was Japan Prime Minister Takaichi Snubbed at China's Big Summit?: The New York Times**
Images from Shenzhen show Sanae Takaichi received a different welcome from other leaders, and some Japanese officials say that was a snub. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/26/world/asia/japan-china-takaichi-snubbed.html)

**Nvidia scandal has put Singapore in U.S. sights. What's at stake for the city-state: CBC**
Singapore is stepping up efforts to stop cloud firms, including one named Megaspeed, from getting around US export controls on advanced artificial-intelligence chips. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/nvidia-singapore-9.7436761?cmp=rss)

## Understanding the Issue: Why a Russian ship hit far from Ukraine may already be stuck
A strike on a Russian ship in the Baltic or the Mediterranean is easy to read as the land war spilling, at random, into other seas. Deutsche Welle's account of those operations points somewhere more specific. Russia has only a narrow strip of Baltic coast, between Finland and Estonia, and uses that water to supply Kaliningrad — a Russian region separated from the rest of the country — and to export oil on what is called a shadow fleet. Ukraine had already struck oil terminals in that same arc, at Ust-Luga and Primorsk, near St. Petersburg. Farther south, a corvette of Russia's Black Sea Fleet could not sail home: Turkey has closed the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, the straits that join the Black Sea to the Mediterranean, so the ship was escorting cargo ships in the Mediterranean instead. Elisabeth Braw of the Atlantic Council told Deutsche Welle this is not a hunt for any tanker selling oil above a price cap; the cargo ship Sparta II, hit off Finland, was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies, and the point Kyiv is making is that it can find such ships in whatever water they are in. Officially the goal is to break logistics; military experts and politicians also read the strikes as a signal of strength toward Western allies before any peace talks. Ukraine has hit far from the front before, including an oil refinery in Omsk, in Siberia, and Russian military facilities in Syria before the Assad government fell in December 2024. When the next report names a ship far from Ukraine, check which of three labels it actually uses — warship, alleged arms cargo, or shadow-fleet tanker — and whether Moscow denies the cargo. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/russia-ukraine-war-extends-to-the-baltic-and-the-mediterranean/a-80054604?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

## Media-literacy note
A court order, a prosecutor's charge, and a minister's claim are three different kinds of statement. The first is a ruling you can read; the second is an allegation still to be tested; the third is an official saying what an investigation found, which is not the same as the file itself. When two governments describe the same dead official in opposite terms, the useful next step is the document each one is willing to publish, not a third summary that blends them. Pick one story from today and open the outlet you did not start with.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **Two-hour daily power cuts now reach ninety-two million people across Iran.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) Iran rations power as winter gas runs short
**What happened (neutral):** Iran has begun rolling electricity cuts of about two hours a day, Al Jazeera reports, across a grid that supplies 92 million people. Mohammad Allahdad, head of the national electricity company Tavanir, told state television that distribution limits would start Sunday because of the fuel supply. President Masoud Pezeshkian has asked people to use less power; in a televised interview with state broadcaster IRIB, the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting, the office lights were off and daylight was let in instead. The country holds part of the world’s largest natural gas field and the world’s third-largest proven oil reserves, yet a United States naval blockade of Iranian ports, sanctions, and strikes on energy sites have left the system short. Government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani warned that the gas gap could reach 430 million cubic metres a day this winter, against about 300 million in earlier years. Saeed Tavakoli, managing director of the National Iranian Gas Company, said four processing plants damaged early in the fighting had cut capacity by 230 million cubic metres a day, of which about 100 million had been restored. The company warned that 11 of Iran’s 31 provinces could struggle, especially Mazandaran, Golestan, and North Khorasan. Pezeshkian told the ISNA news agency that attacks on gas infrastructure had made a hard winter more likely, and told investors on November 21 that Iran faced a “silent economic war” tougher than a war with missiles, the state agency IRNA reported. An Al Jazeera reading of the grid puts about 86 percent of electricity on natural gas, about 7 percent on oil-fired plants, about 5 percent on hydropower, and about 2 percent on nuclear power, mainly the Bushehr reactor. Energy Minister Abbas Aliabadi said in August that war damage had taken 4,200 megawatts offline and that repairs were under way. Shortages and cuts were already happening before the United States and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.

**Context & perspectives:** Tehran has refused Washington’s terms for ending the war, which Al Jazeera describes as stuck. Some gas plants can switch to diesel or fuel oil when gas is tight, which is why a gas shortfall shows up as timed power cuts rather than only as cold homes.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/11/25/iran-rations-electricity-how-deeply-are-us-sanctions-blockade-biting?traffic_source=rss) — how the cuts, the gas gap, and war damage fit together

## Major world stories (3)
### 2) Israeli rivals split on a new strike before a government exists
**What happened (neutral):** Interim Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot are still short of a governing majority, Al Jazeera reports, with a first deadline of December 6 to form a government. Eisenkot’s Yashar bloc has 48 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, Israel’s parliament, 13 short of a majority. Arab parties hold 19 seats and could back him from outside the cabinet. The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism alliance, often called UTJ, has not endorsed either man and could join either side. Likud, Netanyahu’s party, has 46 recommendations from lawmakers after that refusal. Eisenkot has ruled out serving under Netanyahu and wants a unity cabinet in which leadership is shared. On Tuesday, Defence Minister Israel Katz called for preemptive strikes before Iran could finish a chemical-weapons programme he says is already under way. In mid-November, U.S. media reported that Netanyahu sent Mossad chief Roman Gofman to Washington to urge joint strikes, citing intelligence that Tehran was working on chemical weapons. Shin Bet head David Zini, National Security Council chair Shmuel Ben Ezra, and ambassador to the United States Yechiel Leiter are also reported to back new strikes. On November 19, President Donald Trump told Fox News there was “indication that Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio,” and did not commit to military action before the end of the year.

**Context & perspectives:** Netanyahu says Israel needs a government free of what he calls the “taint” of Arab-party participation so it can answer an imminent Iranian threat. Eisenkot has told his party he has seen no imminent threat that requires action before a new government is sworn in. Avigdor Liberman, newly seated on the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee and therefore able to see classified intelligence, said he had seen no justification for new Israeli strikes. Military chief Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir and researchers inside Mossad, the foreign intelligence service, also reportedly see no case for an immediate attack, while defence officials have warned Netanyahu that new strikes could widen into a regional war. Gofman has reportedly argued for renewed action.

This disagreement turns on whether the intelligence shows a threat that cannot wait for a cabinet. Katz’s case is that a chemical-weapons programme is already moving, so waiting is the risk, and that a government tied to Arab parties would be too constrained to act. Eisenkot and Liberman’s case is that people with access to the same secret picture do not see that urgency; Liberman said that if a strike came now, “we’ll know that it’s completely motivated by politics and not security concerns.” Their limit is numerical as well as evidentiary: Eisenkot is still 13 seats short, and UTJ can still tip the math toward Likud. Katz’s limit is that the military chief and Mossad researchers are reported not to share his timetable.

**Questions to consider:** Will a government be in place by December 6, or will a strike be ordered before that date?

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/25/could-netanyahu-take-israel-into-another-war-with-iran-to-cling-to-power?traffic_source=rss) — coalition arithmetic and who is urging or rejecting a strike

### 3) Solomon Islands and Australia sign a security treaty that bars foreign bases
**What happened (neutral):** The Solomon Islands has signed a security treaty with Australia that checks China’s influence in the South Pacific, the Associated Press reports. The New York Times adds that a 2022 Solomon Islands agreement with China had raised concern it could let Beijing place a military presence on the islands, and that the new accord precludes such bases.

**Context & perspectives:** The new text is aimed at one specific fear from that 2022 pact: a Chinese base. The articles do not quote a Chinese response, and they do not say the 2022 agreement itself has been torn up.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/australia-solomon-islands-china-security-treaty-6eaee893cd625ad71bd34dbe887ac73a) — the treaty as a check on Chinese influence
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/24/world/asia/solomon-islands-security-treaty-australia-china.html) — the 2022 China pact and the bar on bases

### 4) Houthis claim hits on a Saudi refinery; Riyadh reports drones down and 11 hurt
**What happened (neutral):** Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen said on Wednesday they had again struck Saudi Arabia, Deutsche Welle reports. Military spokesman Yahya Saree said “accurate and direct” attacks on Ras Tanura — the kingdom’s largest oil refinery and a major crude export terminal — had set fires there, and that an attack on Riyadh’s financial district was “carried out in three phases, with strikes hitting their targets accurately.” Saudi defence officials said air defences shot down four Houthi drones at Ras Tanura, and that 11 people were injured when a tower in the financial district was hit. The same building was struck on November 19, with no injuries then.

**Context & perspectives:** The two accounts do not describe the same result. Saree says the refinery attacks caused fires and that the Riyadh strikes landed as planned, framing them as retaliation in a civil war that has run for more than a decade and has widened with the Iran fighting and tension in the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf’s oil chokepoint. Saudi defence officials say four drones never reached Ras Tanura, and they are the source for the injury count at the tower. Deutsche Welle does not cite an independent check that fires broke out at the refinery. Saree’s strongest reason for treating the operation as a success is his claim of accurate, phased hits on a terminal that matters to oil exports. The Saudi officials’ strongest reason for treating it as a failed raid plus a costly hit is the interception count, plus the fact that the same tower was attacked six days earlier without injuries. Each version leaves a gap the other side would point to: a claimed fire without an outside confirmation, and an interception claim that still sits beside 11 wounded people.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/houthis-claim-attacks-on-saudi-refinery-financial-district/a-80043632?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Houthi claims and the Saudi defence account

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 5) A climate disaster fund has far more requests than cash
**What happened (neutral):** The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, built to help countries recover from climate disasters and slow changes such as rising seas, is already short, Deutsche Welle reports. A first call drew 2.8 billion dollars in urgent requests, with 342 million dollars available. By this summer only about half of the money pledged had arrived. The European Commission signed a 25 million euro contribution agreement on the sidelines of COP31, the latest U.N. climate conference, writing down a pledge first made at COP28. Spain pledged a further 15 million euros. Other loss-and-damage gifts were scarce. The board has provisionally set aside 21.6 million dollars for Nepal after an August glacier collapse that killed more than 1,500 people, with 5,600 more missing. Nepal must still file a request saying how the money will be spent, and an earlier request after Kathmandu floods is already waiting. Pakistan, which pushed the fund onto the agenda after 2022 floods that affected 33 million people and killed more than 1,730, has two projects in and has been told the cap is 200 million dollars. Minister of State for Climate Change Shezra Mansab Ali Khan Kharal told Deutsche Welle Pakistan had still not seen anything on the ground.

**Context & perspectives:** Nepali climate-finance expert Bibek Raj Kandel said asking a country in an emergency to write a proposal adds bureaucracy that does not match the urgency. Kharal said Pakistan does not want a climate disaster to become more debt, and wants grants rather than loans. Abid Qaiyum Suleri, executive director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute in Islamabad, called the promises hollow and said the form of the money matters as much as the sum for a heavily indebted country.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/the-loss-and-damage-fund-exists-but-the-money-doesn-t/a-80035620?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — requests, cash on hand, and who is still waiting

### 6) Japan’s price gauge hits its fastest pace since 2023
**What happened (neutral):** A Bank of Japan measure that strips out fresh food and special factors rose 3.5 percent in October from a year earlier, the fastest pace since September 2023, the Japan Times reports. The Bank of Japan is the country’s central bank. The paper says the reading backs the case for another interest-rate increase.

**Context & perspectives:** The figure is a policy input, not itself a decision to raise rates. No date for a next meeting appears in the report.

**Read more (sources):**
- [The Japan Times](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/2026/11/25/economy/boj-inflation-indicator-hike/) — the October reading and the hike case

## Progress watch (1)
### 7) Bangladesh raises the garment minimum wage by 36 percent
**What happened (neutral):** What’s actually being done is a pay decision, not another round of talks. Bangladesh has raised the minimum wage for garment workers after weeks of protests, the Associated Press reports. Al Jazeera puts the rise at 36 percent. The protests have cost the country hundreds of millions, and workers have not yet accepted the offer.

**Context & perspectives:** The raise is the government’s answer to the walkouts. The open complication is that the people it is meant to pay more have not agreed to it.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/bangladesh-garment-workers-wages-537a1cb23611befc8532408e6b4b1a5d) — the wage rise after weeks of protests
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/25/bangladesh-garment-workers-win-36-pay-rise-after-weeks-of-protest?traffic_source=rss) — the 36 percent figure, the cost of the protests, and the lack of acceptance

### Also Today
**3 Dead and Many More Trapped in Indonesian Mine After Heavy Rainfall: The New York Times**
At least three people are dead and at least 23 workers are believed stuck since Monday in an unauthorized gold mine in Bogor, West Java, after its narrow shaft flooded. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/25/world/asia/indonesia-miners-trapped.html)

**North Korea Kicks Out Swiss Diplomats in Spat Linked to Ukraine War: The New York Times**
North Korea expelled Swiss diplomats after Switzerland sanctioned an international youth camp accused of hosting Ukrainian children for indoctrination. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/25/world/asia/north-korea-switzerland-diplomats.html)

**Iraq’s Prime Minister Aims to Wrest More Power From Kurdistan Region: The New York Times**
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, after a symbolic win against a powerful Iran-backed militia, has moved to assert control over Kurdish border crossings and oil. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/24/world/middleeast/iraq-prime-minister-kurdistan-control.html)

**Mexico Investigates Prosecutor Who Aided the C.I.A. Over Cartel Collusion: The New York Times**
Mexico is investigating a prosecutor, already wanted over his work with the C.I.A. and recently fled to the United States, for suspected collusion with cartels. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/25/world/americas/mexico-prosecutor-cia-us.html)

**Sentences served, but Gaza prisoners remain behind Israeli bars: Al Jazeera**
The Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs says 48 people from Gaza remain in Israeli custody after finishing their sentences, which Palestinian prisoner groups tie to Israel’s Unlawful Combatants Law. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/25/sentences-served-but-gaza-prisoners-remain-behind-israeli-bars?traffic_source=rss)

**Domestic violence soars to record high in Germany: Deutsche Welle**
Deutsche Welle reports a record in which a man kills his wife or ex-partner every three days and police record a sexual offence against a woman every ten minutes, which Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig called a shocking finding. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/domestic-violence-soars-to-record-high-in-germany/a-80041678?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

**South Africa: South Africa Refuses to Drop Empowerment Laws Over U.S.Tariffs: AllAfrica**
Trade Minister Parks Tau says South Africa will not abandon economic empowerment rules under United States tariff pressure, and wants those rules to help more Black owners make goods and sell them abroad. Source: [allafrica.com](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611250230.html)

**Lawmakers call for clarity after HK$4.1 billion clawback from green projects fund: South China Morning Post**
Hong Kong’s legislature passed a bill bringing 4.1 billion Hong Kong dollars of the Environment and Conservation Fund back onto government books, from a March balance of 6.2 billion, leaving 2.1 billion earmarked for the fund’s next operations. Source: [scmp.com](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/health-environment/article/3375769/lawmakers-call-clarity-after-hk41-billion-clawback-green-projects-fund)

**Surprise Eurostar strike cancels London, Paris and Brussels trains: France 24**
A surprise Eurostar strike has cancelled trains among London, Paris, and Brussels. Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261125-surprise-eurostar-strike-cancels-london-paris-and-brussels-trains)
