## Understanding the Issue: How a winter gas shortage becomes a timed power cut
A common misreading is that a country with huge oil and gas reserves goes dark only if the fuel itself has vanished, or that a short daily cut means the whole grid has collapsed. The host’s own explanation of the mechanism is this. In a gas-heavy system, the same fuel often heats homes and turns the turbines that make electricity. In winter, heating demand rises just as the network is least able to spare gas for power stations. Operators then have two scarce things to protect: pressure in the gas pipes, and the steady frequency of the electric grid. If they let every customer draw at once, either the gas pressure falls until more plants trip offline, or the grid frequency slips and larger areas go dark without warning. A rolling cut is a queue. Neighbourhoods, or whole districts, lose power for a set stretch so that hospitals, water plants, and some industry can stay on, and so that the same homes are not dark for the entire day. That is a ration, chosen in advance, not the same event as a storm tearing down lines. It also explains why fixing a damaged turbine does not, by itself, end the cuts: if the missing piece is fuel to burn, a repaired plant still sits idle. When you next read a story like this, separate three lines that are often folded into one: how much generating equipment is broken, how much fuel is actually reaching the plants, and whether the darkness is on a published schedule or arriving without warning.
## Media-literacy note
When two official voices describe one explosion, write down who claims a fire and who claims an interception before you decide which picture you believe. A wage figure, a treaty clause, and a death count are all checkable against the office that issued them, not against the loudest headline. If a story matters to you, open the second link and see which sentence that outlet actually adds.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **More than 6,500 Rohingya face return from Malaysia to Myanmar after a genocide ruling.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) Malaysia sets dates to send Rohingya back to Myanmar
**What happened (neutral):** Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim told parliament that Malaysia will send more than 6,500 Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar, Al Jazeera reported. The announcement came five days after the International Court of Justice — the United Nations’ top court — ruled that Myanmar’s security forces committed genocide against the Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority. Anwar said 1,500 Myanmar nationals will leave on three navy vessels from December 6 to 7, and that 5,303 more will be flown back in December at the Myanmar government’s expense. As of August, the UNHCR — the UN refugee agency — had 225,740 refugees and asylum seekers registered in Malaysia, about 90 percent of them from Myanmar. The United Nations says the Rohingya make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers there.

**Context & perspectives:** CONTESTED. In late September, about 1,500 migrants were sent back in a scheme rights groups called opaque. The court has said Myanmar must allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return of people displaced inside the country or abroad. Anwar said many asylum seekers were victims of atrocities by Myanmar’s regime, that hosting them had become a financial burden and a security risk, and that waiting for other countries to resettle them had not worked. He said talks with Myanmar’s former junta chief, now President Min Aung Hlaing — hosted in Malaysia last month despite rights-group criticism — were meant to protect Malaysia’s interests and fit the court’s call for a safe and dignified return. Rights groups have warned that legitimising that government can endanger people sent back; Malaysia said late last month it would seek clarification of reports that hundreds of recent returnees were in military detention, a request Anwar did not mention in this speech. The South China Morning Post adds a separate limit on outside help: Anwar confirmed Turkey will not take 10,000 Rohingya from Malaysia, which hosts more than 133,000 members of the community and is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention, the treaty that sets international rules for protecting refugees.

The shared legal text is the court’s return order. Anwar’s case is that Malaysia cannot keep carrying the cost and the risk, that third-country resettlement has failed, and that a negotiated return is how a host state gives effect to “safe and dignified” language. The rights-group case is that an opaque earlier transfer, reports of military detention, and official contact with the former junta make “voluntary” and “safe” hard to credit unless the people themselves are choosing to go and someone independent can see what happens on arrival. Anwar has already said many of those in Malaysia were victims of atrocities; the articles do not record a matching concession from the rights groups.

**Questions to consider:** Will the three navy vessels leave on December 6 and 7 with the 1,500 people Anwar named?

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/24/malaysia-set-to-return-thousands-of-rohingya-refugees-to-myanmar-2?traffic_source=rss) — parliamentary figures, court ruling, and Anwar’s case for return
- [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/people/article/3375614/what-next-malaysias-133000-rohingya-after-turkeys-refusal) — Turkey’s refusal and Malaysia’s status outside the Refugee Convention

## Major world stories (3)
### 1) South Korea scrambles jets after Russian planes near Ulleung
**What happened (neutral):** South Korea scrambled fighter jets and briefly told residents of Ulleung Island to take shelter after Russian military planes approached on Tuesday, Al Jazeera reported. The Joint Chiefs of Staff — the country’s top military command — said about five Russian aircraft entered South Korea’s air defence identification zone, a declared buffer that is not the same as sovereign airspace, and came “very close” to the air over Ulleung, home to 9,000 people and 120 kilometres (75 miles) off the northeastern coast. There was no entry into South Korean airspace. Spokesperson Jang Do-young said an intrusion was anticipated, so a warning went out in advance. The Ministry of the Interior and Safety issued a shelter alert at 7:52 a.m. and lifted it three minutes later. North Gyeongsang province first said the jets were suspected to be North Korean, then corrected that.

**Context & perspectives:** South Korea’s Foreign Ministry conveyed regret to Russia and asked for steps to prevent a repeat, but did not summon the Russian ambassador. The Defence Ministry did call in Russia’s military attaché, Nikolai Marchenko, for a formal complaint. Russian aircraft have entered this zone five times this year, including last week, when Japan also protested that two suspected Russian aircraft had entered Japanese airspace. In 2019, South Korean jets fired warning shots after a Russian aircraft entered territorial airspace near Dokdo during a joint patrol with Chinese bombers; Moscow denied a violation then. Moscow has not commented on Tuesday’s flight. The last panic on Ulleung was in 2022, when North Korean missiles triggered sirens. The two Koreas remain technically at war under a 1953 armistice, not a peace treaty — which is why a North Korean label on the alert mattered, and why the correction mattered.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/24/why-s-korea-issued-air-raid-alert-after-russian-jets-flew-near-its-airspace?traffic_source=rss) — timeline of the alert, the correction, and the complaint to Moscow

### 2) World Food Programme warns three sea chokepoints are pricing out aid
**What happened (neutral):** Luke Lindberg, executive director of the World Food Programme — the UN agency that delivers food aid — told the UN Security Council on Monday that disruption at three sea routes is raising food and aid costs, Al Jazeera reported. He called the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab al-Mandeb, and the Black Sea a “triple chokepoint” that has tightened food exports and farming inputs. If current conditions last, the agency expects 727 million dollars in extra costs by mid-2027, which could put assistance for 7.3 million people at risk. He said 266 million people worldwide face acute hunger, with a famine risk in parts of Sudan, South Sudan, and Somalia.

**Context & perspectives:** About 30 percent of global fertiliser supplies pass through Hormuz. The Black Sea is a key grain source for countries including Somalia and Yemen, which imports 90 percent of its food. By mid-October, 63 percent fewer wheat and maize vessels were moving through the Bosphorus than a year earlier. About 10 million tonnes of Russian and Ukrainian wheat could miss global markets, enough, the agency said, to feed an estimated 44 million people. In Sudan, the cost of a basic diet has risen 130 percent since February. Lindberg said grain is available and that the blockage is political, not a failure of production. He asked governments to hold three lines: no more famines, no more use of food as a weapon, and no more attacks on humanitarian workers.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/24/wars-choke-global-food-routes-threatening-aid-for-7-3-million-wfp-warns?traffic_source=rss) — Lindberg’s Security Council figures and the three routes

### 3) US Army says Iowa lead-explosive blasts will go ahead
**What happened (neutral):** The United States Army will blow up a deteriorating stockpile of toxic lead explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, about 240 kilometres southeast of Des Moines, Al Jazeera reported. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said late Monday that going ahead was a “consensus decision” among the federal agencies involved, the courts, and state officials. The plan is two controlled detonations of 68 drums holding almost 4,500 kilograms (10,000 pounds) of degraded lead azide, a chemical used in munitions. A three-judge panel of the 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals lifted an earlier stay on Monday, after President Donald Trump had told the Army to wait until the court ruled in its favour.

**Context & perspectives:** CONTESTED. Everything turns on which danger is larger: a planned blast, or leaving volatile material in place. The Environmental Protection Agency — the US pollution regulator — says a managed detonation is far less risky than a spontaneous explosion, a risk it says grows as Iowa gets colder, and that chemically neutralising the drums or moving them could itself set off an uncontrolled blast. Environmental groups sued to block a special permit, arguing the blasts could send a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops, and livestock well beyond the site. Telle said every expert agency agrees and that Iowa’s current and incoming governors say the call belongs to the experts. Before the stay was lifted, Army lawyers had told the court the service intended to detonate with or without approval, citing an emergency exemption from federal environmental law. The groups’ suit treats that permit, and the reach of any dust, as the point the experts have not settled. The articles do not quote the groups conceding the cold-weather risk, or the EPA conceding how far a plume might travel.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/24/us-army-says-detonation-of-lead-explosives-in-iowa-will-proceed?traffic_source=rss) — Telle’s decision, the court stay, and the permit fight

### 1) Chinese carmakers pass Japanese rivals in six more markets
**What happened (neutral):** Chinese carmakers now hold a larger market share than Japanese rivals in 26 markets, the South China Morning Post reported, citing preliminary data from the American firm Mobility Global. They overtook Japanese competitors in six new markets this year, including Brazil, Ghana, Italy, South Korea, and Tunisia. **Context & perspectives:** The comparison is about who sells more cars in those markets, not about a government treaty or a factory opening. The sixth new market is named only in part in the text available here, so it is not listed. Higher energy prices are the mechanism the report offers for why electric vehicles are taking share from Japanese brands that still sell many fuel-burning models.

**Read more (sources):**

### 2) Pakistan’s Zeeshan Ali joins China’s station crew
**What happened (neutral):** China on Tuesday named the crew for Shenzhou-24, and a Pakistani payload specialist is set to become the first foreign astronaut aboard Tiangong, China’s space station, Deutsche Welle reported. Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, a former Pakistani air force pilot, will fly with Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi. The China Manned Space Agency said the launch from Jiuquan, in the Gobi Desert, is set for 8:18 a.m. local time on Wednesday (0018 GMT). Ali said he carries “the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis.”

**Context & perspectives:** Al Jazeera, citing the agency’s spokesperson Zhang Jingbo, said this is the first joint flight by Chinese and foreign astronauts in China’s crewed programme. After a rendezvous of about three and a half hours, the craft is to dock at the Tianhe core module. Ali’s stay is short: Deutsche Welle says about five days, and Pakistan’s space agency, SUPARCO, told Al Jazeera about a week. He returns on Shenzhou-23, which docked in May, while Zhu Yangzhu of that crew stays up for a year. He will run China-Pakistan experiments in biotechnology and materials, including cyanobacteria, which are photosynthetic microbes. The Globe and Mail adds that the flight rests on an agreement signed in February 2025, that Tang, 51, will be the first person to board Tiangong three times, and that labels on the station are in Chinese, so Ali trained in the language from almost no base. He is not the first Pakistani in space: Namira Salim flew a Virgin Galactic mission in October 2023. Pakistani ministers called the seat a mark of 75 years of space cooperation. China aims to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030; the United States is aiming for 2028.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/pakistani-astronaut-to-join-chinese-space-mission/a-80028922?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — crew naming, launch time, and Ali’s remarks
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/24/pakistans-zeeshan-ali-set-for-historic-flight-to-chinas-space-station?traffic_source=rss) — docking plan, experiment list, and SUPARCO’s duration
- [The Globe and Mail](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-china-unveils-crew-for-historic-space-mission-with-pakistani-astronaut/) — 2025 agreement, Tang’s record, and language training

**Context & perspectives:** The money and the labour came from the families who use the school, not from a new national pledge. Occupation is the result that can be checked: children are in the blocks, not waiting on a groundbreaking.

**Read more (sources):**

## Understanding the Issue: A return order is not a ban on sending people back
People often hear a genocide judgment and assume every country must keep the survivors and must refuse every flight home. That mixes three different jobs. What follows is the host’s own explanation of the mechanism, not a finding from a single document in today’s list.

A court can decide that a state’s forces committed genocide and can order that state to allow people to come back in safety, of their own choice, and with dignity. That order binds the state that was sued. It does not, by itself, give every other capital a new duty to house those people forever.

A second rule sits in the refugee treaty: a country that has joined it generally may not push someone back to a place where they face serious harm. A country that never joined does not carry that treaty duty in the same way, even if its officials still talk about safety and choice.

“Voluntary” is the hinge. A voluntary return is a person’s decision, not a bus timetable set by the host and the country they fled. “Safe” and “dignified” are conditions on the receiving state — papers, no punishment for having left, somewhere to live — not a slogan either government can stamp on a passenger list.

Coverage that says a return “fits” a court ruling is using the court’s adjectives. Coverage that says people are being removed after a genocide finding is using the direction of travel. Both can be literally true and still hide whether anyone asked the passengers.

When you next read a return story, look for two checkable things the adjectives do not replace: a record that the people agreed, and the name of someone independent who will see them after they land.

## Media-literacy note
When two outlets cover the same decision, read the paragraph that carries a number before you read the paragraph that carries a motive. A court order, a parliamentary sentence, and a rights-group warning are three kinds of claim; each can be accurate and still answer a different question. If a figure matters to you, open the document or the speech it came from, not only the headline that borrowed it.

**Go deeper:** Al Jazeera reports Anwar’s December ship and aircraft counts and the UNHCR registry totals; the South China Morning Post reports Turkey’s refusal to take 10,000 people and that Malaysia never joined the UN Refugee Convention.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **Seven naval drones sank Russia's Merkury in Libya, extending Ukraine's war far past the Black Sea.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) Ukraine says drones sank a Russian warship in a Libyan port
**What happened (neutral):** President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces used seven domestically made naval drones to sink the Russian corvette Merkury — a small warship — at Benghazi port in Libya in the early hours of Sunday, CNBC reported. He called the Merkury one of Russia's newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war, and posted video of an explosion. CNBC said the strike also damaged the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to move weapons, and destroyed a Ka-27 military helicopter on the corvette. Satellite imagery taken Sunday, CNBC reported, showed the Merkury mostly underwater and capsized. The Security Service of Ukraine, the SBU, said the attacks showed that Russia's military fleet and logistics have no safe routes even far beyond the Black Sea. The same CNBC account placed the strike beside a suspected Ukrainian drone hit on a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea on Saturday.

**Context & perspectives:** The United Nations Support Mission in Libya, UNSMIL, said it was seriously concerned, warned that Libya cannot afford to become a battleground for foreign conflicts, and called for an immediate, independent, and transparent investigation. The Kremlin did not immediately answer CNBC; the Guardian's Europe live blog reported that, asked about the reports, the Kremlin said information would come from Russia's Defence Ministry. On the cargo ship, the outlets do not agree. CNBC reported that Zelenskyy said the MV Angara was damaged, and the New York Times reported that he said drones sank the corvette and hit the dry cargo vessel. The Guardian's live blog reported that Zelenskyy said the Angara was also sunk. The satellite finding CNBC cites is about the Merkury, not the Angara.

This is a contested claim about what the strike was for, and about what should follow.
Zelenskyy called it an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war, and said Ukrainian forces would continue operations in designated waters. The SBU said such operations destroy logistical capacity and force Russia to pay for aggression even at a strategic distance from Ukraine.
UNSMIL's case is about Libya, not about who is winning the sea war: a foreign strike in a Libyan port pulls a country that is not a party into someone else's conflict, so the facts should be established independently and those responsible held to account. Neither Kyiv nor UNSMIL, in these reports, conceded the other's point. Moscow has not yet given its own account.

**Read more (sources):**
- [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/23/ukraine-russia-warship-libya.html) — Zelenskyy's account, the seven drones, the helicopter, and the satellite image
- [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/nov/23/russia-ukraine-war-zelenskyy-libya-benghazi-drone-attack-ship-merkury-un-nato-europe-latest-news-updates) — live blog; says Zelenskyy described the Angara as sunk, and records the Kremlin's referral to the Defence Ministry
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/world/europe/ukraine-libya-russian-ships.html) — corvette sunk, cargo vessel hit
- [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/23/g-s1-155017/ukraine-attack-russian-warship-libya) — Zelenskyy's claim that sea drones sank the warship

## Major world stories (3)
### 1) UN climate summit ends with no agreed cover text
**What happened (neutral):** The UN climate summit known as COP31 — the Conference of the Parties, the annual meeting where governments try to agree a shared climate text — ended in Antalya, Turkey, without a consensus cover decision, CNBC reported. The meeting had opened on November 9. After talks ran almost two days past schedule, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and others rejected a draft that did not mention fossil fuels. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was deeply disappointed that no consensus was reached. France24 reported that the final agreement was rejected on Sunday after record overtime. More than 90 countries did back a separate pledge to raise electricity's share of global final energy use from about 23 percent to about 35 percent by 2035, CNBC reported.

**Context & perspectives:** Talks had also covered funding for developing nations and how to respond to scientific warnings, including that the 1.5 degrees Celsius temperature target is likely to be overshot. Ireland's climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the EU, told Reuters the conference was hijacked by some oil states when asked about Saudi Arabia's role; CNBC said it had contacted Saudi Arabia for comment. The EU said the text does not respond to the science and that it will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels. The UK government said the presidencies' text does not meet the moment and moves backward on the science. Philip Davis, prime minister of the Bahamas, said that three years ago in Dubai nations agreed to transition away from fossil fuels, that small island states produce less than 1 percent of global emissions, and that Antalya exhausted their patience. Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, called it the worst COP ever and said rich countries blocked a just transition mechanism. Albert Salamanca of the Stockholm Environment Institute Asia told CNBC the lack of consensus was tantamount to a death sentence for vulnerable communities still unable to respond in time. The World Wildlife Fund said the lack of progress on finance for developing nations has real-world consequences for the most vulnerable. Nonsikelelo Nkomo-Mabobe of Solidaridad welcomed food-security language in the proposed Antalya Pact but said a finance gap remains and that funding must be easier for frontline communities to access and traceable once disbursed.

The draft's failure is contested, and the named split is over what the failure was.
The shared ground is narrow and factual: there is no adopted cover decision, and the rejected draft did not mention fossil fuels. From there the accounts diverge.
The EU's reason for voting the text down is that a cover decision which never names fossil fuels would launder the status quo and ignore the science. Davis ties that to a promise already made in Dubai, and to islands that emit very little and live with the damage.
Adow's reason is different. He argues the decisive blockage was not only missing fuel language but rich countries stopping a just transition mechanism, which he describes as abandonment of developing nations. Nkomo-Mabobe, who works on fair supply chains, did not treat the whole text as empty: she said food-security wording was a promising sign, and still said the money is neither easy to reach nor easy to trace.

**Read more (sources):**
- [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/23/cop31-climate-summit-fossil-fuels.html) — the rejected draft, the EU and UK positions, the electricity pledge, and named reactions
- [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261123-the-worst-cop-ever-climate-talks-collapse-in-chaos) — Sunday collapse after two days of overtime
- [AllAfrica / IPS](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611230241.html) — no final cover decision after countries did not agree a text that explicitly mentions moving away from fossil fuels

### 2) Oxfam says contamination covers nearly all of Gaza
**What happened (neutral):** A report by the charity Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory, CEOBS, says Israel's use of explosives and incendiary weapons has caused environmental contamination across more than 99 percent of Gaza, Al Jazeera reported. The enclave has about 2.3 million people. Oxfam international executive director Amitabh Behar said military assaults on the environment are environmental war crimes that threaten life now and for generations, and that Palestinians are exposed through air, food, water, and contact with contaminated soil and debris. Al Jazeera reported that the assault has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, and that more than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since a ceasefire was signed in October 2025.

**Context & perspectives:** The report uses satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis, and other open-source data. It points to the highest concentrations in Gaza City, Jabalia, and the North Gaza governorate. A study cited in the report estimated direct conflict emissions at more than 1.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent by January 2025. By October 11, 2025, Oxfam estimates, Israeli ground operations had directly affected about 283 square kilometres of Gaza's 365 square kilometres, or 78 percent. The UN Environment Programme estimates 61 million tonnes of debris since October 7, 2023, about 29 tonnes of rubble per person living in Gaza now. More than 90 percent of Palestinians have been forcibly displaced, most of them more than once. Oxfam estimates the rubble would take 2.1 million dump-truck loads to clear, which it equates to 736 trips around the planet. In September 2025 a UN international commission of inquiry said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. The International Court of Justice is hearing a genocide case; in January it said it was plausible that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Behar said the destruction would breach Israel's legal obligations if it has degraded the conditions needed for human safety. Oxfam said a full independent investigation is needed to identify and reduce the risks. The articles provided here do not include an Israeli government response to this report.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/23/environmental-crimes-israel-blamed-for-toxic-pollution-in-99-of-gaza?traffic_source=rss) — the Oxfam and CEOBS findings, casualty and debris figures, and the call for an investigation
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/video/newsfeed/2026/11/23/gaza-turned-into-toxic-wasteland-by-israels-war-says-new-report?traffic_source=rss) — short video report on the same study

### 3) NATO meets after Russian missiles fell in Poland
**What happened (neutral):** German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said on Monday, as the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly continued in Berlin, that the alliance will defend every centimetre of NATO territory, Deutsche Welle reported. NATO is the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, the defence alliance of 32 countries. Addressing Russian President Vladimir Putin, Wadephul said the alliance is defensive but prepared to defend its countries. Polish state prosecutors said the three objects that crashed in southeastern Poland on Friday were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the latest violation an intentional provocation. It came during a wide-ranging Russian attack on Ukraine and at the same time as European military drills in Poland.

**Context & perspectives:** Representatives of NATO members were also due to meet in Brussels on Monday to discuss the Polish airspace violations. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte was expected to address the Berlin assembly around midday local time, then attend a reception with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was due to speak to the assembly by video link. Wadephul said he was in close contact with Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski and assured Warsaw of full solidarity. The Guardian's Europe live blog reported that Poland is expected to ask allies for further military support, and that the UN Security Council will meet to discuss Russian attacks on civilian targets, including the consulates of Austria and the Netherlands in Kyiv. Deutsche Welle reported that Russian drones and missiles have repeatedly entered Polish airspace during strikes on Ukraine, and that violations have also been reported in Romania, Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia. On Saturday, Finland reported a suspected violation by a manned Russian military helicopter near Loviisa. Moldova, which is in neither the EU nor NATO, also reported a violation this weekend.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/nato-parliamentary-assembly-convenes-amid-russian-airspace-violations/live-80016415?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Wadephul's remarks, the Kh-101 finding, and other reported violations
- [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/nov/23/russia-ukraine-war-zelenskyy-libya-benghazi-drone-attack-ship-merkury-un-nato-europe-latest-news-updates) — Poland's expected request for support, and the UN Security Council meeting on civilian attacks

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 1) Ghana's employed population has more than doubled since 1992
**What happened (neutral):** The number of employed people in Ghana has more than doubled over the past 35 years, from six million in 1992 to 13.3 million in 2025, AllAfrica reported, citing the Ghanaian Times on a Ghana Statistical Service report. The GSS is the national statistics office. Most of those workers remain in the informal sector, the part of the economy where jobs are typically outside formal contracts and protections.

**Context & perspectives:** The report, as described, raises concerns about job security, earnings, and working conditions even as the headcount of employed people has grown. The headline on the Ghanaian Times account says productivity has risen while workers' earnings have lagged. The summary provided here does not give a separate productivity percentage or a wage figure.

**Read more (sources):**
- [AllAfrica](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611230262.html) — the GSS employment figures and the informal-sector concern

### 2) A lab test finds rule-breaking spreads more easily than good examples
**What happened (neutral):** In an online experiment led by Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same, Deutsche Welle reported. Researchers recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election. Participants watched an animated shooting star cross 100 squares and were told to click where it shone brightest, always near the middle. Squares farther right paid more, so cheating paid. Choosing alone, they picked the farthest-right square — the most blatant violation — about 23 percent of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40 percent of the time. Small violations had only a small effect. Just over 4 percent went further than the person they had watched. Seeing someone stick to the rule rarely changed what others did.

**Context & perspectives:** The task had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished. Each person chose first, then saw what a previous participant had done and which party that person supported, and could change their answer. The task was repeated six times. Some people followed the rule every time, and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. In computer simulations that placed digital versions of the participants in groups of 100, the handful prone to escalating sometimes pushed the whole group toward heavy rule-breaking. Molleman said a few bad actors like these can take off the guardrails of the group.

The dispute is about what kind of spread this is.
Molleman's reading follows the mechanism in the numbers: a blatant break by someone on your own side moved the extreme cheat from about 23 percent to almost 40 percent, while a good example barely moved anyone, and a small share then went further than the person they copied. On that account, guardrails fail from the bad example, not from the absence of a good one.
Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews who was not involved, told the Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He noted that people who see a riot often turn up afterward to help clean up.
Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved, told Science News that the lack of punishment matters, because punishment and social pressure also shape whether rule-breaking spreads, and that is not how the world works. The study itself already shows a limit on simple copying: some participants never moved, no matter what they saw.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/rule-breaking-is-contagious-and-good-examples-barely-help/a-79980025?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — the Amsterdam experiment, the percentages, and the outside critiques

## Progress watch (1)
### 1) Liberia concludes a power-and-road deal with a gold miner
**What happened (neutral):** Liberia's government has concluded a 5.7 billion dollar infrastructure deal with Bea Mountain Mining Corporation, AllAfrica reported, citing the Liberian Investigator. The terms would add 270 megawatts of electricity through four new power plants — more than three times the capacity of the Mount Coffee hydropower plant — and build a 146-kilometre highway.

**Context & perspectives:** The deal would be paid for largely with extra revenue the gold miner owes as gold prices rise. That is the main complication: the new plants and the road are still to be built, and the money described here depends on gold prices staying high enough to produce that extra revenue.

**Read more (sources):**
- [AllAfrica](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611230226.html) — the concluded deal, the megawatts, the highway, and the gold-revenue funding

### Also Today
**Bangladesh vows to arrest ex-PM Hasina if she returns from India: The Hindu**
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said Dhaka expects India to honour the extradition treaty, as Sheikh Hasina's planned December return fuels political tension and street violence. Researchers tracking HIV in rural KwaZulu-Natal say all four indicators they analysed show that momentum against the epidemic has been lost, and that it could start growing again. Source: [allafrica.com](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611230203.html)

A UN court decision against Myanmar sets a precedent in international law with implications for a similar case over Israel's actions in Gaza. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/world/genocide-myanmar-un-climate-talks.html)

Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez stepped down with immediate effect after admitting Capita has not delivered for retired civil servants left waiting for pension payments, and the share price plunged 67 percent; chief financial officer Pablo Andres replaces him. Customs arrested two people and seized about 120,000 suspected counterfeit items worth an estimated 68 million Hong Kong dollars, in 38 cases of goods intended for transshipment during the Double 11 shopping peak. Criminal Court C ordered the permanent seizure of electronic devices taken from former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor's Congo Town residence, and warned that a further violation of her conditional medical release could return her to Monrovia Central Prison. A World Bank study published in June 2017 warned that West African container traffic would at least double by 2025 and that existing terminals could not absorb it without new capacity; Liberia built no new terminal, and ships now queue off Monrovia as the National Port Authority pushes a 230 million dollar terminal. Carlos Alcaraz beat Alexander Zverev 6-2, 7-6 (9-7) on Sunday for his first ATP Finals title, joining Roger Federer, Andre Agassi, and Novak Djokovic as men who have won all four majors and the ATP Finals. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11/23/carlos-alcaraz-atp-finals-2026-title-alexander-zverev-tennis?traffic_source=rss)

Kano State governor Abba Kabir Yusuf said Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso sent him to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu to pledge that they would join the All Progressives Congress if they won at the Supreme Court after the 2023 governorship dispute. Source: [allafrica.com](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611230271.html)

## Understanding the Issue: Why a climate text can die without a vote
People often picture a climate summit as a legislature: a text is drafted, countries vote, and the majority wins. That is the wrong picture of the main political statement.
What follows is this host's own explanation of the mechanism, not a finding copied from one of today's articles.
The overarching statement at these summits is adopted by consensus. In practice, that means the text goes through only if no participating government blocks it. There is no simple show of hands that lets a large majority overrule a holdout.
Because the rule is consensus, the argument is about the words that every government will put its name to, not about which side has more flags in the room. A paragraph one bloc will not accept can sink the whole cover text even when many other governments wanted that paragraph in.
Narrower promises work differently. A group of countries can announce a pledge among themselves without every government signing the summit's single cover text. A news report can therefore be true that "a deal failed" and also true that "dozens of countries backed a separate target." Those are not the same document.
That split is the useful test. When you next read that a climate meeting succeeded or collapsed, check which paper is being described: the consensus cover text, which needs near-universal acceptance, or a coalition pledge, which does not.
Source line omitted: this section is the host's own explanation.

## Media-literacy note
When two reputable outlets describe the same speech, compare the verb. "Damaged," "hit," and "sunk" are not interchangeable, and only one of them may match what was shown. On a summit, separate the document that needed everyone's consent from the pledge a smaller group announced on its own. Primary statements — a president's post, a UN mission's note, a court order — are worth more than a headline's summary of them. If a report names no response from the government it accuses, say that the response is absent, and do not invent one.

**Go deeper:** CNBC reports that Zelenskyy said the cargo ship MV Angara was damaged, and the New York Times says it was hit; the Guardian's Europe live blog says he said the Angara was sunk. The satellite detail CNBC cites shows the Merkury mostly underwater, not a finding about the Angara.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **Nearly two hundred nations weigh a draft that admits one point five degrees will be passed.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) A new COP31 draft still omits fossil fuels as overtime runs on
**What happened (neutral):** Diplomats from nearly 200 countries are still in Antalya, Turkey, on a second day of overtime at COP31, the United Nations climate summit, after a Friday close slipped, Deutsche Welle reports. The latest draft still does not mention fossil fuels, the main driver of human-caused warming. Al Jazeera reports that the new draft would, for the first time, acknowledge that global warming is on course to pass the 1.5C threshold. German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider called the draft “not acceptable” and “a step backward from previous decisions on climate protection.” Former Greenpeace chief Jennifer Morgan said it would be better to end with no deal than with a text that “sets us back,” and that “Saudi Arabia’s fingerprints are all over” the draft. She also said this year’s Turkish presidency was “not well prepared” and had left four days of shuttle diplomacy with no text.

**Context & perspectives:** CONTESTED. The dispute turns on whether a thin text is better than none. The Turkish COP presidency has suggested it is better to accept the current draft than to leave with no resolution at all — a finished line, even a weak one, keeps nearly 200 governments inside one decision rather than scattering them. Schneider’s case is that a conference whose only job is climate protection cannot adopt a text that moves backward from earlier decisions; Germany, he said, cannot support that. Morgan’s case, aligned with the German minister, is that a decision which vulnerable islands and people reject would set the process back, and that oil-producing states shaped the omission. She praised Germany for refusing the text and contrasted this presidency with last year’s Brazilian one, which she said had spent the year pulling countries together. Deutsche Welle also notes fossil fuels are the flashpoint while energy prices are high and the US-Israeli war with Iran continues. The summit stays open until there is consensus, or until governments choose to leave without one.

**Questions to consider:** Will Antalya close with an adopted text or with no decision at all?

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/cop31-fossil-fuels-still-missing-from-draft-deal-at-un-climate-summit/live-79999516?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Schneider and Morgan on a draft that still omits fossil fuels
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/22/fossil-fuel-impasse-pushes-cop31-climate-talks-into-second-day-of-overtime?traffic_source=rss) — new draft would note warming on course past 1.5C

## Major world stories (3)
### 1) Cost-of-living marches continue across Europe, with two very different French counts
**What happened (neutral):** Sunday is a third straight day of protests from Portugal to France over the cost of living and affordable housing, France24 reports, after large demonstrations on Friday and smaller ones on Saturday; in France the marches have now run for six weekends. Al Jazeera reports that organisers counted 150,000 people in France on Saturday, down from 200,000 the week before and from 800,000 on October 17, the first of the weekly demonstrations. France’s Ministry of the Interior said turnout had “significantly declined,” putting Saturday at 82,500, compared with 106,000 a week earlier. The two counts are not reconciled in either report: organisers and the ministry are measuring the same Saturday and publishing different totals.

**Context & perspectives:** Al Jazeera reports the movement began in mid-September with high school students calling for better learning conditions, then widened into a national campaign over prices, public services, and police brutality. Marches have been largely peaceful, with sporadic violence at the edges and repeated accusations of police brutality. Last month, the same weekly rallies produced the worst rioting in years, with hundreds of shops looted and buildings attacked and set on fire. Unions and activists have called for more protests in the coming weeks. No government reply to those demands is quoted in today’s reports.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/11/22/photos-people-rally-across-france-over-living-costs-public-services?traffic_source=rss) — organiser and interior-ministry turnout figures
- [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/europe-sees-new-protests-over-rising-costs-inequality-and-public-services) — third day, from Portugal to France
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/video/newsfeed/2026/11/22/clashes-erupt-across-france-in-another-night-of-protest?traffic_source=rss) — police moved to disperse crowds Saturday night

### 2) Somalia expels the UAE ambassador after years of security cooperation
**What happened (neutral):** On November 19, Somalia ordered the United Arab Emirates’ ambassador to leave and recalled its own envoy from Abu Dhabi, Al Jazeera reports — the sharpest break yet with a partner President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud once called “one of the greatest pillars” of the war against al-Shabab, the al-Qaeda-linked armed group. The UAE said it had already withdrawn its diplomatic staff from Mogadishu in January. The expulsion came 10 months after Somalia annulled commercial, defence, and security agreements, accusing Abu Dhabi of undermining its sovereignty.

**Context & perspectives:** CONTESTED. Mohamud’s own framing, two days before the order, was familial and absolute: “A brother does not burn your house. A brother does not buy your property without your knowledge. A brother does not divide your family.” National security adviser Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed wrote that, after years of engagement, the federal government judges UAE policy a threat to national security — financing rival regional administrations and armed actors outside federal control. The strongest case for the break is that a state cannot fight al-Shabab, or hold a federation together, if a wealthy partner arms and funds the regions that resist the centre. Anwar Gargash, a senior Emirati official, answered that ties “remain deeper and stronger” despite the criticism, and that Mogadishu is letting its internal political disputes strain the relationship — a case that the president’s fight with semi-autonomous regions, several of them close to Abu Dhabi, is being exported into foreign policy. Abu Dhabi’s foothold grew in Mohamud’s first term, 2012 to 2017: the embassy reopened in 2014, and he inaugurated a UAE-funded military training centre the next year, while the UAE also built commercial and security ties with Puntland, Jubbaland, and Somaliland, which declared independence in 1991. The UAE remains a major trading partner and a hub for Somali businesses. Neither side, in this account, spells out which annulled agreements still bind anyone.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/22/why-somalias-president-turned-against-his-former-ally-the-uae?traffic_source=rss) — expulsion, annulled agreements, and the two governments’ accounts

### 3) Indonesia searches for about 50 people after a Java factory fire
**What happened (neutral):** Indonesian police recovered seven body bags on Sunday while rescuers searched for about 50 workers still missing after a fire tore through a factory in western Java, the South China Morning Post reports. Firefighters were still hitting hotspots more than a day after the blaze. Police said one body bag might hold body parts from several people. The heat left the recovered dead unidentifiable by sight, so authorities are collecting DNA from relatives.

**Context & perspectives:** The search and the DNA collection are the response named so far. The reports do not give the factory’s name, the cause of the fire, or a full death toll.

**Read more (sources):**
- [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast-asia/article/3375375/indonesia-searches-50-recovers-7-body-bags-after-factory-fire) — seven body bags and a search for about 50

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 1) South Korea’s education minister resigns after exam-day phone alerts
**What happened (neutral):** President Lee Jae Myung has accepted the resignation of Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin, the BBC reports, after last-minute steps to stop cheating tools threw Thursday’s Suneung — the annual college entrance exam, taken by about 500,000 students — into confusion. A week earlier, Han Won-seok, top scorer on the national tax accountancy exam, admitted using a microcamera, a phone, and an AI tool; he got one of 160 questions wrong. Choi told Yonhap he could not escape criticism that the ministry “failed to prepare in advance.” The ministry said 111 candidates were found with unauthorised smart devices. For the first time, the national disaster-alert system was used to catch cheaters: three alerts between 08:00 and 15:00 local time made phones sound even on silent, including tourists on data roaming, unless the phone was off or in airplane mode. Candidates had to cover shirt and jacket buttons and submit eyewear to inspection.

**Context & perspectives:** France24 also reports the Sunday resignation, centred on that tax-exam admission. Lee has been calling for an overhaul of the exam system. Students told local media they feared ordinary glasses would be treated as smart glasses; one wore contact lenses to avoid suspicion. The Suneung can last up to nine hours and shapes careers for millions of South Koreans.

**Read more (sources):**
- [BBC](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw3dgk29d37no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss) — resignation accepted, 111 devices, disaster alerts
- [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/south-korea-ai-cheating-sparks-exam-security-chaos) — minister quits ahead of the entrance exam

### 2) Kenya weighs mandatory internet meters
**What happened (neutral):** A bill before Kenya’s National Assembly would make consumption-based internet billing mandatory, Al Jazeera reports. The Kenya Information and Communications (Amendment) Bill, 2025, sponsored by Aldai MP Marianne Jebet Kitany, would require each customer to have a unique meter number, with providers monitoring use, turning it into readable detail, and billing by consumption. Providers would also send billing-system information, including meter numbers, to the Communications Authority of Kenya at least once a financial year. The stated aim is to stop unfair billing so people pay for the data they use. The bill does not expressly require recording message content or websites visited.

**Context & perspectives:** The Communications Authority has urged lawmakers not to make metered billing compulsory. Telkom Kenya has warned of consequences for privacy, affordability, and investment. Demas Kiprono of the International Commission of Jurists Kenya argues the regulator already can handle billing complaints, and questions whether identifiable usage records are necessary and proportionate. Critics want the text to say who may see the records, how long they are kept, and when they may be shared. Kenya’s Data Protection Act, 2019, already governs personal information; opponents want Parliament to say how it would apply here. The assembly’s Departmental Committee on Communication, Information and Innovation is considering the bill.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/22/kenyas-internet-metering-bill-raises-privacy-and-affordability-concerns?traffic_source=rss) — meter numbers, regulator and civil-society objections

## Progress watch (1)
### 1) Rhine cargo capacity returns as gauges climb out of the lows
**What happened (neutral):** Germany’s Federal Institute for Hydrology expects water in large western rivers, including the Rhine, to return to average or above in the next few days after sustained rain, Deutsche Welle reports. At Kaub, near Koblenz — a bottleneck on the Middle Rhine — the gauge could reach some 3.3 metres, more than 3 metres above the last low-water readings. The Weser and Danube are also expected to rise, with smaller increases on the Elbe and Oder. Fabian Spiess, deputy manager of the inland navigation association BDB, said each ship again has much more cargo capacity. The complication he names is that mid-year load cuts caused losses that will not be made up soon; in 2018, a similar low-water year, better months at the end did not repair the damage. A conservation NGO said the rain is temporary relief and does not undo harm to amphibians and water insects in small, moist habitats.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-ig-metall-union-calls-for-new-24-hour-strike/live-80008430?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Kaub gauge, shipping capacity, and the dry-period limit

### Also Today
**Nepal PM Balendra Shah heads to Delhi for first bilateral visit: Deutsche Welle**
Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, is due in New Delhi for a two-day visit, his first bilateral trip since taking office in March, with a Monday meeting with India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, expected to centre on rebuilding after August floods that left some 1,500 dead, more than 5,200 missing, and a reconstruction bill Nepal puts at $4.78 billion. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/india-nepal-pm-balendra-shah-heads-to-delhi-for-first-bilateral-visit/live-80008104?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

**China and Vietnam finish a Gulf of Tonkin naval patrol: South China Morning Post**
China and Vietnam completed a two-day joint naval patrol in the Gulf of Tonkin on Saturday, lasting 32 hours and 351 nautical miles, even as their South China Sea claims still overlap. Source: [scmp.com](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3375372/pla-anti-submarine-ships-conduct-south-china-sea-patrol-vietnamese-navy)

**ICE arrests two people on a Seattle airport jet bridge: Deutsche Welle**
Masked immigration officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and Sofia Hernandez Mejia on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday as passengers boarded for Los Angeles; Governor Bob Ferguson called the footage horrific, and Alaska Airlines said it had no advance notice. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/us-ice-arrests-2-at-seattle-airport-in-chilling-scenes-governor/a-80012480?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

**Indian opposition youth wing warns of more Meta protests: The Guardian**
The youth wing of India’s Congress party warned of further protests after members clashed with police on Friday outside Meta’s offices in Hyderabad over the removal of some members’ accounts. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/22/india-congress-meta-protests-police-hyderabad)

**China’s ambassador calls Serbia an ironclad friend: South China Morning Post**
Ambassador Li Ming told the Belgrade paper Politika that China and Serbia were “ironclad friends,” as the Student List prepares to take power and look hard at major public projects, including those involving Chinese firms. Source: [scmp.com](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3375340/despite-serbias-political-earthquake-china-hopes-ties-will-stay-rock-solid)

**IG Metall calls another 24-hour strike: Deutsche Welle**
Germany’s largest union, IG Metall, is launching another 24-hour strike on Monday for car and shipyard workers as a pay dispute escalates. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-ig-metall-union-calls-for-new-24-hour-strike/live-80008430?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

**Dashcam shows a missile strike in Lviv: Al Jazeera**
A Friday Russian attack struck a residential neighbourhood in Lviv, in western Ukraine, killing two people and damaging infrastructure. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/video/newsfeed/2026/11/22/dashcam-captures-russian-missile-strike-on-lviv-ukraine?traffic_source=rss)

**Displaced Palestinians protest as strikes continue in Gaza: Al Jazeera**
A Gaza mayor said Israeli forces are still destroying residential buildings as part of a “gradual displacement” policy, while displaced Palestinians protest. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/22/displaced-palestinians-protest-as-israeli-air-strikes-continue-in-gaza?traffic_source=rss)

**Bessent says he is still living on a US military base: Al Jazeera**
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he is still living at a US military base, two weeks after an Israeli warning tied to Iran fears. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/video/newsfeed/2026/11/22/bessent-confirms-hes-living-on-us-military-base-over-iran-fears?traffic_source=rss)

**Minnesota farmer says wolves killed three calves as protections are reconsidered: Fox News**
Farmer Shayne Isane said gray wolves killed three calves in one night, costing thousands of dollars, as President Donald Trump moves to reconsider federal protections. **Logging and climate change reshape Canada’s boreal forest: The New York Times**
Canada has presented preservation of its boreal forest as a model, while commercial logging combined with climate change is inflicting severe damage, The New York Times reports. **Theresa May tells Andy Burnham to move on from Brexit: The Guardian**
Theresa May said she was aghast at talk of rejoining the European Union and wished Andy Burnham had not reopened Brexit, while Reform UK’s Richard Tice called Friday’s agreements a reverse that would cut GDP and the government said they could add 0.5 percent. India’s Gukesh Dommaraju defends the world title against Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov in Geneva from November 22, with both players 20 at the first classical game on November 24 — the youngest world championship match on record — over up to 14 games and a shared $2.5 million prize fund. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11/22/gukesh-vs-sindarov-the-youngest-world-chess-championship-in-history?traffic_source=rss)

**English village holds a symbolic vote to “leave” the UK: France24**
Residents of Barnham voted on Saturday in a symbolic referendum to leave the United Kingdom, protesting plans to house 931 asylum seekers at a former air force base, more than the village’s population of 584. Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/english-village-votes-to-leave-uk)

**Kenya’s internet metering bill draws privacy objections: Al Jazeera**
Aldai MP Marianne Jebet Kitany’s bill would require unique internet meter numbers and consumption billing; the Communications Authority does not want that made compulsory, and the International Commission of Jurists Kenya questions whether identifiable usage records are necessary. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/22/kenyas-internet-metering-bill-raises-privacy-and-affordability-concerns?traffic_source=rss)

## Understanding the Issue: How sending an envoy home differs from tearing up a treaty
People often hear “the ambassador was expelled” and picture a treaty torn in half. That picture mixes three different acts. What follows is the host’s own explanation of the mechanism, not a claim drawn from today’s articles. Under the Vienna rules that most capitals still use, a receiving state may declare a diplomat persona non grata — no longer welcome — and the sending state is expected to withdraw that person; the embassy as an institution can remain, sometimes with a lower-ranking chargé d’affaires. Recalling your own ambassador is the mirror move: you pull your representative without necessarily closing the building or ending trade. A third act, annulling a named defence or commercial agreement, is a legal step of its own and has to say which contract dies. Staff can also be gone for months before an expulsion order is issued, which means the public rupture and the practical absence of diplomats need not fall on the same day. Reading today’s coverage, the useful split is between a political signal — who is allowed to stay in the capital — and a legal inventory of which contracts still bind. Next time an expulsion leads the news, look for a list of cancelled agreements separate from the sentence that sends the envoy home; if that list is missing, the legal relationship has not been described yet.

## Media-literacy note
When two institutions count the same crowd, write down both numbers and who produced each before you pick one. A draft climate text is a primary document: the presence or absence of a single phrase is the fact, and a minister’s rejection is a separate fact. Diplomatic quotes travel well as slogans; the checkable piece is which agreements were annulled, and on what date.

**Go deeper:** Deutsche Welle reports that the Antalya draft still does not mention fossil fuels and that Germany’s environment minister calls it unacceptable; Al Jazeera reports that the new draft would, for the first time, say warming is on course to pass 1.5C.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **Denmark gives Russia's defence attaché seven days to leave after an alleged kill plot.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) Denmark expels a Russian defence official over an alleged murder plot
**What happened (neutral):** Denmark’s security and intelligence service, PET, says Russian intelligence planned and started an attempt to kill a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, the BBC reports. Danish media name him as the rapper Kyivstoner; his real name is Albert Vasiliev. PET says it stopped people who meant to kill him at a September concert. Three people were stopped in a car near the venue on September 25, and firearms and knives were in the vehicle. Two people have been charged with attempted murder and with assisting a foreign intelligence service; both pleaded not guilty. PET says the people were tied to Loyal to Familia, a banned Danish gang it describes as known for serious violent crime. Foreign minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said Russia’s defence attaché — the officer who represents a military at an embassy — must leave within seven days, and he called the alleged attempt intimidation meant to make Denmark waver in its support for Ukraine. He also wants the European Union, the bloc of European states, to limit Russian travel: a Schengen visa, the short-stay visa that usually lets a visitor move across much of Europe, should count only in the country that issued it. Russia’s embassy called the allegations unsubstantiated and said Copenhagen gave no evidence of Moscow’s involvement. Russian state media, citing the foreign ministry, say Moscow will answer the expulsion. On Saturday, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen — the head of the European Union’s executive — said she condemned an assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence, and called it an attack on European Union soil.

**Context & perspectives:** In July, Russia’s FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organizing a terrorist attack on military facilities and personnel in Russia; he denied that on social media. France 24 reports that Danish authorities have also announced tighter restrictions on visas for Russian tourists, beside the expulsion.

**Contested:** Rasmussen’s case is that the plot was pressure on a government backing Ukraine, not a private quarrel: armed men were stopped near a concert, linked by PET to a banned gang, after Russia’s own security service had already accused the performer. Von der Leyen treats that as an attack on European Union soil and says Russia’s hybrid threats — mixes of covert and open pressure — are becoming less hybrid and more real. The embassy’s case is that Denmark has not shown Moscow’s hand. It says a “Danish model” has appeared, in which a “Russian trace” is found and used for a propaganda spectacle, to frighten Danes and justify a long confrontation. The two charged people have pleaded not guilty; the embassy does not accept the intelligence claim, and Copenhagen has not, in the embassy’s telling, produced the evidence it asked for.

**Questions to consider:** Will European Union governments take up Denmark’s request that a Russian short-stay visa work only in the country that issued it?

**Read more (sources):**
- [BBC](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmde1lj4yjxno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss) — PET’s account, the charges, the expulsion, and the visa request
- [France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261121-unacceptable-eu-chief-condemns-alleged-russian-plot-to-kill-us-ukrainian-citizen) — von der Leyen’s condemnation
- [France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/denmark-accuses-russia-of-assassination-plot-expels-diplomat) — expulsion and tighter tourist-visa limits

## Major world stories (3)
### 1) Iran says it shot down a US drone as Hormuz talks stay stuck
**What happened (neutral):** Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a branch of its armed forces, said on Saturday that a new air-defence system shot down a US MQ-9 drone — an uncrewed US military aircraft — over the Strait of Hormuz, Al Jazeera reports, citing Iranian state broadcaster IRIB. The Guard said it was the 58th US MQ-9 brought down by Iranian forces. The strait is the narrow sea lane through which, in peacetime, one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas passed. The war, launched by the United States and Israel on February 28, has killed thousands, disrupted shipping, and pushed energy prices higher. A June memorandum of understanding was never fully carried out because the two sides disagreed on freedom and security of navigation; attacks have resumed from time to time since July. In August, The Washington Post reported that the United States had lost 45 MQ-9 drones, about 25 percent of that fleet, at a cost of more than $1.3 billion, during combat operations in Iran. On Friday the US Treasury said it had sanctioned four Iranians it called “oil trustees,” people it says collected money from illicit oil sales to evade sanctions and a naval blockade. Among them are Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former Guard intelligence officer, and Majid Taj, brother of Iranian Football Federation president Mehdi Taj.

**Context & perspectives:** Foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday that seven conditions Iran sent the United States in September “must be implemented for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen,” including an end to the war and the lifting of sanctions and the naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports. He said Iran would negotiate how to carry those conditions out, that the timetable was “flexible,” and that talks depended on American confidence-building steps. He ruled out sending Iran’s stockpile of 60 percent enriched uranium abroad, but said a “fair solution” could be reached and that some mediator proposals were “worth examining.” He called the current “no war, no peace” state undesirable, and said Iran could not accept a deal that would “hand victory to the other side.” At the White House the same day, President Donald Trump said Tehran wants a deal, but not one acceptable to him: “We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal that they’ve been doing for 51 years.” He had said last week that a deal to end the war was unnecessary. Vice President JD Vance, who had blamed the war for Republicans losing both chambers of Congress this month, declined to say whether he would have authorized the February strikes to stop Iran developing a nuclear weapon. He said that decision was Trump’s, and that his job was to support the president.

**Contested:** The split is what must happen before ships move freely again. Araghchi’s case is that reopening Hormuz is the last step, not the first: end the war, lift sanctions and the blockade, then talk about the timetable, with room for mediators on the uranium stockpile but no transfer of that 60 percent material abroad, and no text that declares the other side the winner. Trump’s case is that Iran’s offer is the old pattern under a new name — a deal he will not sign — and that Washington does not need an agreement to end the war. Vance did not claim the February strikes as his own call.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/irans-irgc-downs-us-drone-over-hormuz-as-efforts-to-end-war-remain-stalled?traffic_source=rss) — the drone claim, Hormuz conditions, and Friday’s sanctions

### 2) Paris court jails three officers for the 2020 beating of Michel Zecler
**What happened (neutral):** A Paris criminal court has convicted three police officers of intentional, racist violence in the 2020 assault of Michel Zecler, a Black music producer, and of falsifying a police report, Al Jazeera reports. Aurélien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, were each sentenced to five years in prison, part of it suspended, and barred from the police. Zecler, 47, co-founded the independent rap label Black Gold Corp. Officers stopped him outside his Paris studio on November 21, 2020, accusing him of not wearing a face mask required under COVID-19 rules, then pushed him inside. Over about five minutes they punched, kicked, and used batons for some 30 blows. He suffered head trauma and a complete rupture of a biceps tendon. The presiding judge said the officers had been dishonest in their report to shield themselves from discipline and the law, with no regard for the criminal consequences Zecler faced. Lapersonne, who filed the report, had claimed Zecler struck out with his arms and legs; asked if he had made that up, he told the court, “Absolutely.” He said he left the officers’ blows out of the report out of fear. All three admitted excessive force and apologized. They denied racism. The judges said Zecler’s account — that he heard the slur “sale negre” — had been consistent, and that the false report damaged the officers’ credibility. The New York Times reports that security cameras filmed the beating and that it set off a national backlash.

**Context & perspectives:** Music journalist Olivier Cachin told the French paper Sud Ouest that Zecler works in the background and is not a “look-at-me” type. Tondeux said he regretted “the image I have given of the police.”

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/french-police-officers-guilty-of-michel-zecler-assault-what-happens-now?traffic_source=rss) — verdict, injuries, and what was said in court
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/three-french-police-officers-sentenced-over-racist-assault-on-black-man?traffic_source=rss) — racism treated as an aggravating factor
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/world/europe/france-police-brutality-black-producer.html) — the filmed beating and the national backlash

### 3) Three Salvadoran soldiers die in Haiti as a prison deal is announced
**What happened (neutral):** Three Salvadoran soldiers were killed in Haiti while handling explosives, El Salvador’s military said on Friday, Deutsche Welle reports. It is the first officially reported deaths since a 2,000-member Salvadoran contingent was sent last month to the gang-hit Caribbean country. One soldier died while being treated in the neighboring Dominican Republic, where he had been airlifted. Another was wounded and is out of danger. The military did not say where the blast happened or what explosives the soldiers were handling. President Nayib Bukele sent the troops to rescue four Salvadoran airmen — members of the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force — who went missing after a gang ambush on October 18 in Port-au-Prince. Those extra troops are not part of that force, and the job has widened toward Haitian gangs. On Friday, Haiti announced an agreement with El Salvador to build three new prisons, after security and justice minister Patrick Pelissier visited El Salvador. A Salvadoran company will build them with a Haitian firm, he said. Haitian prisons are notoriously overcrowded; in 2024, gang raids on two of the biggest freed thousands of inmates.

**Context & perspectives:** Pelissier visited El Salvador’s maximum-security Terrorism Confinement Center, known as CECOT, and praised it: “Once you enter, there is no hope of ever seeing the outside world again.” El Salvador has imprisoned more than 90,000 people, with no family visits, since a state of exception began in 2022. The military said it extended condolences to the three families.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/three-el-salvador-soldiers-die-in-explosives-accident-in-haiti/a-80008005?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — the deaths and the three-prison agreement

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 1) Geneva agrees to “elaborate” killer-robot rules by 2028, not to negotiate a ban
**What happened (neutral):** The 128 countries at a United Nations conference in Geneva have agreed to “elaborate” a possible accord on lethal autonomous weapons — machines that can kill without a human making the final decision to fire — over the next two years, Al Jazeera reports. The Saturday decision came under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, a treaty on weapons considered especially harmful. Nearly 100 nations had pushed for swift, legally binding rules. The United States, Russia, and Israel opposed that push. The convention decides only if every member agrees. Diplomats said Russia’s objections on procedure led to some formal sessions being called off, and talks on the final wording ran through the night. Swiss chair Julien Thoeni said some countries rejected the word “negotiate,” so the text says “elaboration” instead. Reuters headlines the same decision as talks aimed at regulating these weapons by 2028.

**Context & perspectives:** Thoeni said more than ten years of talks had produced a significant step for humanitarian disarmament, and that the process should decide which weapons international humanitarian law — the rules for protecting civilians in war — can ban, and which it can permit but regulate. Stop Killer Robots, a coalition of 300 organizations, called the mandate “watered down” and said it offered no clear route to binding rules. Executive director Nicole van Rooijen told Agence France-Presse that autonomous weapons are already in combat, including systems that use artificial intelligence to choose targets, and that delaying a binding instrument puts civilians at risk. Verity Coyle, deputy director for arms at Human Rights Watch, told the agency the outcome was disappointing and did not provide the urgent action needed, “but the technology is racing ahead.”

**Contested:** Everyone in the room is arguing about weapons that can pick a target and fire without a person making that last call, under a treaty that cannot move unless every member says yes. Van Rooijen’s case for a binding ban now is that the machines are already being used, so a slower paper exercise leaves civilians exposed while software improves. Coyle’s addition is urgency: a mandate that does not force new rules loses the race to the technology. Thoeni’s case for the wording that passed is that “elaborate” was the verb objectors would sign, after “negotiate” was rejected, and that a unanimous step after a decade still lets states sort bans from regulated permissions. The United States, Russia, and Israel opposed the faster, binding route; Russia’s procedural objections were enough to cancel some formal sessions because one member can stop the convention.

**Questions to consider:** When the elaboration is written, does it name any weapon that must be banned, or only a process for talking further before 2028?

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/nations-agree-to-draft-rules-for-killer-robots-at-arms-control-summit?traffic_source=rss) — the “elaboration” mandate, the holdouts, and the critics
- [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/states-agree-to-un-talks-aiming-regulate-killer-robots-by-2028-2026-11-21/) — the 2028 horizon in the headline

### 2) An Anthropic mathematician says Claude helped prove a 167-year-old prime-number claim
**What happened (neutral):** Levent Alpoge, a mathematician on the technical staff of Anthropic, an artificial-intelligence company, says he used the company’s Claude tool to produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Deutsche Welle reports. He posted the claim on his website on Friday: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.” The hypothesis, stated by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, is about how prime numbers — numbers divisible only by themselves and 1 — are spaced as they get larger. It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems chosen by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers $1 million for a solution to each. Alpoge said the work with the system generated more than 250,000 pages, and that he had not yet mastered all the mathematics involved. He wrote that Claude “far outpaced me near the finish line.” The proof still has to be checked by other mathematicians. Martin Bridson, president of the Clay institute, called the announcement one of historic significance in a statement quoted by the Associated Press, and said it holds the promise of a dramatic change in what people think is possible in mathematics. He added: “But the journey from today’s announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult.”

**Context & perspectives:** In September, OpenAI said its technology had helped with a problem on the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe how fluids such as water and air move — another of the seven prize problems. That claim also still needs independent checks. Confirming Riemann’s pattern would matter for a wide range of further mathematical work, Deutsche Welle reports; until other mathematicians sign off, it remains a claim, not a settled theorem.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/anthropic-researcher-uses-ai-to-solve-math-s-greatest-riddle/a-80008428?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Alpoge’s claim, the prize, and Bridson’s caution

## Progress watch (1)
### 1) A US judge approves Bayer’s Roundup payouts, up to $7.25 billion
**What happened (neutral):** A judge in Missouri has approved a settlement under which Germany’s Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion, about €6.6 billion, over the next two decades to resolve US lawsuits from people who say they should have been warned that the weedkiller Roundup could cause non-Hodgkin lymphoma, Deutsche Welle reports. The deal applies nationwide. People already ill, and people who develop the cancer later, could receive an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, depending on how they used the product, their age at diagnosis, and how severe the illness is. Deutsche Welle reports that some lawyers say the payments are too low. The decision could be appealed.

**Context & perspectives:** The approval is a completed court result, not a promise of a future fund: money is now allocated against thousands of claims, with the appeal risk still open and with critics of the sums already on the record.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/us-judge-approves-bayer-s-7-25-billion-cancer-settlement/a-80007474?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — the judge’s approval

### Also Today
**Germany news: Support for Ukraine military aid waning, survey shows: Deutsche Welle**
A YouGov survey taken November 13–16 for Welt am Sonntag found 49 percent of people in Germany want Berlin’s financial, military, and humanitarian aid to Ukraine reduced or cut, including 25 percent who want it dropped, while 30 percent want it kept and 9 percent want it raised.
