**Houthis launch strikes on Saudi Arabia: France 24**
The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles fired toward Riyadh early on Saturday, the second Houthi attack on the Saudi capital in recent days, after Saudi-led strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen. **Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says: BBC**
Foreign secretary Ed Miliband said the wider UK-EU reset is not dependent on a tuition-fees deal, after Brussels sources had suggested the bloc might withhold the wider package until fees for European Union students in Britain were lowered, and he said rejoining could be examined among “all options.” Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9w9p4geke8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Bangladesh minister vows action against those behind arson, blames Awami League-linked groups: The Hindu**

Source: [foxnews.com](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/2028-presidential-contender-under-fire-from-state-auditor-over-waste-fraud-abuse-fears-troubling-response)

## Understanding the Issue: Why one country’s visa is not a private key to the whole continent
A common picture of European travel is that a short-stay visa is a national courtesy, so the country that stamps it can later shrink it to its own borders by itself. What follows is this host’s own explanation of the mechanism, not a finding from today’s articles. The Schengen system is a shared external door: most European Union countries, plus a few neighbors, dropped routine checks on the borders between them and kept checks on the outside edge. A short-stay visa is usually issued by one state but written for the whole area, because the point of abolishing internal controls was that a visitor cleared once should not be stopped at every next frontier. The issuing country does the paperwork and is supposed to be the main destination, yet the document is not that country’s private pass. Any state on the external border can still refuse entry if the traveler fails the common conditions — purpose, funds, return, security flags — even with a visa in the passport. That is a refusal at the door, not a rewrite of the visa’s map. Changing the map, so that a visa issued in one capital works only there, is a change to a shared instrument. It needs the states that issue the common visa to agree, because a Dane who cannot issue a Europe-wide visa also cannot, alone, un-issue the Europe-wide visas other capitals have already printed. Reading a demand to “limit Russian travel” against that mechanism means asking which lever is actually being pulled: tighter national practice at one window, refusals at the border, or a rule change that rewrites where the visa is valid. The check, next time a government says it will confine a Schengen visa to one country, is whether the text is a national instruction to its own consulates or a proposal the other issuing states still have to adopt.

## Media-literacy note
When two governments contradict each other on a plot, write down the charge, the denial, and the piece of evidence each one actually offers — a seized weapon, a named agency, a missing document — before you adopt either story. A court verdict and a diplomatic accusation are not the same kind of fact: one has a judgment you can read, the other is a claim until charges are tested. For a scientific announcement, the useful next document is the proof other specialists can check, not the press line that a famous problem has fallen. If you read only one outlet on a contested expulsion or a stalled negotiation, you are reading one capital’s file.

**Go deeper:** The BBC reports the firearms and knives in the car, the banned-gang link, and Rasmussen’s request that Russian short-stay visas count only in the issuing country; France 24 adds von der Leyen’s line that this was an attack on European Union soil, and reports that tighter limits on visas for Russian tourists have been announced, which is a step beyond a request still sitting with the bloc.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **Up to half a percent of GDP is what Britain's Treasury ties to today's EU reset.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) Britain and the EU tie a post-Brexit reset to a later fight over tuition fees
**What happened (neutral):** British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is in Brussels to announce a deal resetting Britain's relationship with the European Union, the bloc it left a decade ago, The New York Times reports. He is meeting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa. France24 reports the two sides are hoping to strike several deals meant to open closer cooperation. The Guardian reports that European Union sources say today's reset will not take effect without a further agreement on tuition fees for European Union citizens, a decision senior diplomats had already put off for six months. During a meeting with businesses, Burnham said the sides were "pretty much there, and it's a really good deal," and that Treasury analysis out today puts the gain at up to 0.5 percent of British gross domestic product, which he called the single biggest growth intervention in this Parliament.

**Context & perspectives:** The tuition-fee condition is the lever. European Union sources told The Guardian that deferring the fee level was meant to give London leverage in parallel talks on "Made in Europe" legislation, rules designed to protect European supply chains against China. Making the food-and-drink deal contingent on fees is described by those sources as a way to neutralise that leverage. France, The Guardian reports, insisted last night that Britain could not have voting rights on food-and-drink legislation. Al Jazeera reports London is signalling a willingness to align more closely with the European Union on various policies.

The dispute turns on whether a reset announced today is a finished bargain or a bargain the European Union can still reopen. Burnham's case is that the package is essentially done and is the largest growth step this Parliament, on the Treasury's own figure. The European Union sources' case is that warmth toward a former member is compatible with holding the food-and-drink terms until fees are settled, so London cannot spend the next six months trading access for supply-chain concessions. France's limit on voting rights is the part of that case already stated in public: closer rules, without a seat on the legislation.

**Questions to consider:** Will the text published from Brussels state that the food-and-drink terms wait on a tuition-fee agreement?

**Read more (sources):**
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/world/europe/uk-eu-summit-brexit.html) — Burnham in Brussels to announce a reset deal a decade after Britain left.
- [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261120-brussels-london-eye-reset-deal-at-burnham-s-eu-summit) — Summit with von der Leyen and Costa, with several deals hoped for.
- [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/nov/20/uk-eu-european-union-brexit-deal-andy-burnham-latest-news-updates) — Fee condition, France on voting rights, and the Treasury's growth figure.
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/20/eu-and-britain-to-agree-steps-towards-relations-reset?traffic_source=rss) — London signalling closer alignment on policy.

## Major world stories (3)
### 1) Russian strikes hit Kyiv's bridges; Poland says a missile struck its southeast
**What happened (neutral):** Russia hit three bridges over the Dnipro River in Kyiv and killed eight people in one of the largest air attacks of the war, the BBC reports, days after Ukraine damaged the Crimean Bridge. Ballistic missiles struck the Podilsko-Voskresensky, Darnytskyi and Southern bridges, which were closed to traffic. Ukraine's air force told the BBC that Russia launched almost 100 missiles and about 400 drones. Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said 28 people were injured. Al Jazeera, citing Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi, reported the same toll: eight killed, including six in Kyiv, and 28 wounded. The BBC reported two of the dead at the Sknyliv railway station in Lviv. Deutsche Welle reported an earlier city count from Mayor Vitali Klitschko of at least three killed and 13 injured in the capital. France24 reports Poland said no one was hurt after a Russian missile hit southeast Poland during the attack on Ukraine. The BBC reported a projectile landed about 45 kilometres, or 28 miles, from the border. Deutsche Welle reported Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski saying investigators were at three sites — Rudnik nad Sanem, Molodycz and Nowy Lipowiec — and Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying there was no danger from the air.

**Context & perspectives:** President Vladimir Putin had said retaliation for the Crimean Bridge strike would be "far more painful." Russia's Defence Ministry told Al Jazeera the Kyiv road and rail bridges were targeted because they carry weapons and military equipment, and that energy and transport sites were also hit. First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said nuclear plants cut operations, causing outages in Kyiv and 10 regions. Klitschko asked people not to drive into the city unless necessary and asked employers to allow remote work where they can. The BBC said the barrage began hours after European leaders, including Burnham, President Emmanuel Macron and Chancellor Friedrich Merz, said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow. Al Jazeera reported Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov later saying a visit by three European Union representatives to Russia is "under consideration," while any Ukrainian membership of NATO remains unacceptable to Moscow.

**Read more (sources):**
- [BBC](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6x29gn4pdn9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss) — Eight killed, three bridges closed, missile and drone counts, Poland site.
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/20/russia-unleashes-retaliatory-barrage-on-kyiv-bridges?traffic_source=rss) — National toll, energy cuts, Russian military account, Ryabkov.
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-updates-kyiv-targeted-by-missile-strikes-bridges-hit/live-79999822?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Klitschko's earlier toll and Poland's three investigation sites.
- [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261120-poland-says-russian-missile-hit-its-territory-during-attack-on-ukraine) — Poland says a missile hit its southeast and no one was hurt.

### 2) Baghdad strikes a deal with Kataib Hezbollah over an alleged oil-smuggling ring
**What happened (neutral):** Iraq has reached a compromise with the Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi readied security forces to move against the group, France24 reports, citing three senior security officials. Officials had accused the group of running a smuggling ring that siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil. Under a deal brokered by senior Shi'ite political leaders to avert a confrontation, government forces were expected to move into the group's stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday.

**Context & perspectives:** The sequence in the France24 account is a prepared security move, then a political bargain to stop that move becoming a clash, then an expected entry into the stronghold the next day. The article does not quote Kataib Hezbollah's response.

**Read more (sources):**
- [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261120-iraqi-forces-strike-compromise-with-powerful-pro-iran-militia) — Compromise, oil-smuggling accusation, and the expected move into Jurf al-Sakhar.

### 3) Bukele registers for another term after El Salvador drops presidential term limits
**What happened (neutral):** President Nayib Bukele registered his candidacy on Thursday at the Supreme Electoral Tribunal, Al Jazeera reports, after his party Nuevas Ideas used its supermajority in Congress to remove presidential term limits and extend terms from five years to six. Last year the same majority abolished second-round votes and brought national elections forward by two years, to February 2027. The 45-year-old is widely expected to win on the political support from his crackdown on violent cartels. Last month he sent about 2,500 soldiers to Haiti after four Salvadoran members of a United Nations-backed force went missing; Al Jazeera says Port-au-Prince welcomed that deployment.

**Context & perspectives:** What the constitution now allows, and what that does to competition, is the split. Bukele told the crowd, "In El Salvador there is total, complete open democracy," and "We're sending a message to the world that El Salvador will never return to the past." His stated reason is the break with the cartel violence of that past, and the article says the crackdown is why he is widely expected to win. Juan Pappier of Human Rights Watch, quoted by The Associated Press in Al Jazeera's account, said Bukele is seeking a third consecutive term "after packing the court, rewriting the constitution to his liking and jailing or forcing into exile those who dare criticise him," and that "the absolute concentration of power in his hands has been the defining feature of his administration." The Bertelsmann Transformation Index is cited as accusing him of a de facto one-party state. Al Jazeera also reports that many analysts question the Haiti deployment, saying he is using that crisis to enhance his reputation — a limit attached to the export of his security model, not a concession from Bukele himself.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/20/el-salvadors-bukele-seeks-third-term-after-constitution-change?traffic_source=rss) — Registration, term-limit change, February 2027 vote, and the competing accounts of democracy.

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 1) COP31 draft drops fossil fuels, with a Friday deadline still open
**What happened (neutral):** Australia, co-host of the COP31 United Nations climate talks in Turkey, unveiled a draft agreement on Thursday that drops any mention of fossil fuels, France24 reports. Nearly 200 countries have until Friday to strike a final text, though these talks often run long. Deutsche Welle reports the meetings have been in Antalya since November 9, that an earlier draft this week included a fossil-fuel phaseout, and that Thursday night's text omits gas, oil and coal. The summit is taking place during a record-breaking El Niño, climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal, and an energy shock from the Iran war, France24 reports.

**Context & perspectives:** Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, nations pledged to move away from fossil fuels with no target or timeline, Deutsche Welle reports. Last year's COP30 in Brazil ended with no mention of fossil fuels. Oil- and gas-producing countries have strongly resisted putting that issue back on the table. France's ecological transition minister, Monique Barbut, called the omission a "black mark." Harjeet Singh, convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, said, "You cannot solve a fossil fuel crisis by pretending we don't need to phase out fossil fuels." Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, said the slimmed text had "gone backwards." Australia's climate minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations, said, "We will be consulting and negotiating until it is very clear to us that we have a consensus."

Campaigners and Barbut treat naming coal, oil and gas as the only honest response to a crisis those fuels drive. The producing countries' recorded position is resistance to reopening a phaseout that Dubai left without a date. Bowen's stated rule is that the text moves only when the nearly 200 parties can live with it — which is how a line that was in an earlier draft can leave the later one.

**Questions to consider:** Does Friday's text, or an overtime text, put fossil fuels back in?

**Read more (sources):**
- [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261120-outcry-as-fossil-fuels-scrubbed-from-draft-un-climate-deal) — Thursday draft drops fossil fuels; Friday is the stated deadline.
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/cop31-un-climate-summit-enters-final-phase-with-no-deal-in-sight/live-79999516?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Earlier draft included a phaseout; Bowen, Barbut, Singh and Adow.

### 2) Lufthansa tells staff it will cut 1,000 jobs at Frankfurt and Munich
**What happened (neutral):** Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, Deutsche Welle reports, citing a company letter seen by the German news agency DPA and other outlets. The letter was reportedly signed by chief executive Jens Ritter and four other board members. In the first nine months of the year the airline recorded an operating loss of 180 million euros, about 197 million dollars. The board said the loss averages 20 million euros a month and that this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful. The letter said Lufthansa "is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity." At the end of 2025 the group employed about 67,100 people, up 1 percent from the year before.

**Context & perspectives:** The same letter sets other cuts: employee travel benefits, fewer crew overnight stays abroad, and less short- and medium-haul flying by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets. It also plans to fit ten aircraft a month with Starlink satellite internet and to charge for onboard access. Deutsche Welle reports the timing of the job cuts is unclear, and that it is unknown whether they are part of a September 2025 plan to slash 4,000 administrative posts through artificial intelligence and digitalisation. Rising fuel costs from the US-Israeli war with Iran are cited as a further strain. The article does not name a union response.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/lufthansa-to-cut-1-000-jobs-citing-ongoing-losses-reports/a-80000062?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Job cuts, monthly losses, fleet and internet plans.

## Progress watch (1)
### 1) Hong Kong's public-housing wait falls to a low not seen in more than a decade
**What happened (neutral):** Hong Kong's waiting time for standard and light public housing fell to 4.4 years in the 12 months to the end of September, from 4.8 years at the end of the previous quarter, the South China Morning Post reports — the shortest composite wait in more than 10 years. The Housing Bureau said on Friday that the composite wait, covering both types of public housing, declined across urban areas, extended urban areas and the New Territories. The wait is still measured in years, not months.

**Read more (sources):**
- [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/society/article/3375226/hong-kongs-waiting-time-public-housing-its-shortest-more-10-years) — 4.4 years, down from 4.8, across three district types.

### Also Today
**Spain's leaders clash before next week's election: France24**
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez acknowledged "mistakes" in a televised debate with his main conservative rival, clashing over the economy, housing, immigration, corruption, foreign policy and policies toward women, before an election next week that could leave the far right on the cusp of power. Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261120-spain-s-leaders-clash-over-corruption-economy-in-tense-election-debate)

**Malaysia agrees to resettle 10,000 Rohingya in Turkey: The Hindu**
Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said the Cabinet agreed to resettle 10,000 Rohingya refugees from Malaysia to Turkey through a skills course of three to six months, a day after the International Court of Justice said Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. Source: [thehindu.com](https://www.thehindu.com/news/international/malaysia-plans-to-resettle-10000-rohingya-in-turkiye/article71723939.ece)

**Pakistani climate minister arrives in Delhi: Al Jazeera**
Musadik Malik became the first Pakistani federal minister to visit India since the neighbours' four-day war in May 2025, for a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation forum, with no bilateral meeting announced and India's spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal saying New Delhi's Pakistan policy is unchanged. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/20/pakistan-minister-visits-india-for-first-time-since-2025-war?traffic_source=rss)

**Xi calls the Australia relationship a turnaround: Deutsche Welle**
President Xi Jinping told Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, that they had brought about a "comprehensive turnaround" since 2022, after China had imposed import curbs worth 13 billion dollars that it has mostly lifted. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/china-s-xi-praises-turnaround-in-relationship-with-australia/a-79999229?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

**Troops from 11 countries drill in Poland: AP News**
European troops from 11 countries are drilling in Poland for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine. Source: [apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/poland-ukraine-military-exercise-peace-france-britain-a28d60d1b37093199dd017472028d7ac)

**South Korea catches 111 exam-takers with banned devices: BBC**
Authorities caught 111 students with banned smart devices during the Suneung university entrance exam. Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3vgw1xevvwo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Mamdani sets 2032 as the goal to empty Rikers: The Guardian**
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a plan to end incarceration at Rikers Island by the end of 2032 and said the plan invests 146 million dollars in supports aimed at breaking cycles of incarceration. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/rikers-island-closure-plan-mamdani)

**Cyclone Akvan crosses India's east coast: Deutsche Welle**
Cyclone Akvan made landfall near Gopalpur with winds of 70 to 80 kilometres per hour, gusting to 90, and Odisha had moved more than 300,000 people to relief camps, with no major damage reported so far. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/india-pakistani-minister-visits-delhi-for-sco-forum-amid-frozen-ties/live-79999264?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

**Wreck of Australia's first home-built warship is shown: The New York Times**
The wooden gunboat Spitfire, sunk in a cyclone in 1898, has been revealed in waters near the Great Barrier Reef, 128 years later. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/world/australia/shipwreck-warship-spitfire-great-barrier-reef.html)

**Eurozone negotiated wages edge up: The Wall Street Journal**
Negotiated wage growth in the eurozone accelerated to 2.57 percent in the third quarter from 2.45 percent in the previous quarter, the European Central Bank said. Source: [wsj.com](https://www.wsj.com/economy/global/eurozone-wage-growth-accelerates-but-remains-modest-729eb0ed?mod=rss_worldnews)

**A Lilongwe mini-grid opens: AllAfrica**
Malawi's energy minister, Jean Mathanga, backed more off-grid power as the Lundu mini-grid opened in Lilongwe, toward a stated goal of lifting electricity access from 25.9 percent to 70 percent by 2030. Source: [allafrica.com](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611200294.html)

**UK retail sales rise after a stock-up appeal: Reuters**
British retail sales rose 0.7 percent in October, beating forecasts, after the government told households to stock up. Source: [reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/uk-retail-sales-rise-07-october-beating-forecasts-2026-11-20/)

## Understanding the Issue: Why a growing clean-power share can still leave fossil fuels in charge of energy
People often hear "renewables are booming" and picture coal, oil and gas already shoved to the edge of the energy system. Deutsche Welle's look at whether the Paris temperature limit can still be met shows a split between two different measurements. In 2015, governments agreed in Paris to do what they could to stop the world overheating. Since then, coal, oil and gas have fallen to a record-low share of global primary energy — all the energy supplied, not just what comes out of a socket — and they still account for around 86 percent of that supply. Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told Deutsche Welle, "We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century." Electricity is the faster-moving slice: wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34 percent of global electricity production in 2025, and an Ember analysis found that record solar growth last year meant clean energy met all new global electricity demand, so new fossil generation was held back. Maslin said about 2 trillion dollars is going into new renewable projects, twice the investment in fossil fuels. The United Nations now says overshooting the Paris temperature threshold is inevitable, and that the time spent above it should be kept as short as possible, with heating brought back down by the end of the century, because a longer overshoot raises the risk of self-reinforcing changes such as large-scale forest die-back and melting permafrost. A summit sentence about "phasing out" or not naming fuels at all is a political line; the checkable companion is whether a cited figure is primary energy, still mostly fossil, or electricity, where the clean share is larger and rising faster. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/have-we-missed-our-chance-to-stop-climate-change/a-79986199?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

## Media-literacy note
When two official counts of the same night differ, write down who gave which number before treating either as the full toll. A draft text and a signed deal are not the same object: look for what was removed between drafts, and for what a government says must still be agreed before today's announcement takes effect. Primary documents — a court registration, a housing-bureau table, a company letter quoted in full — beat a headline that collapses a condition into a finished result.

**Go deeper:** The New York Times reports Burnham is in Brussels to announce a reset deal; The Guardian adds that European Union sources say today's deals will not take effect without a later tuition-fee agreement, and it is the Guardian that carries the Treasury figure of up to 0.5 percent of GDP.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **Four of twenty-six points is what aid groups now give Gaza’s peace plan.**

## Today's lead story (1)

### 1) Aid groups score the Gaza peace plan four of twenty-six
**What happened (neutral):** One year after the United Nations Security Council endorsed the Trump administration’s 20-point Comprehensive Plan to end the Gaza Conflict, five aid organisations graded that plan at four of 26 possible points, Al Jazeera reported. The Danish Refugee Council, the Norwegian Refugee Council, Oxfam, Refugees International and Save the Children gave it zero on humanitarian access and one point on civilian protection. The plan bars territorial occupation and requires Israeli forces to withdraw. The Israeli military “Yellow Line” — the boundary Palestinians are not allowed to cross — has instead moved west. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, the UN office that tracks humanitarian conditions, known as OCHA, put Israeli control at 58 percent when the ceasefire began 13 months ago and at 65 percent now. Israel has said it controls 70 percent; a UN official told the Security Council that in June. OCHA said last month that about 2.1 million Palestinians were confined to 128 square kilometres, about 16,000 people per square kilometre. A more recent map analysis by NPR put the area at 109 square kilometres, nearly 19,300 people per square kilometre. Agencies said at least 1,650 Palestinians have been killed and 5,975 wounded since the ceasefire declared in October last year. This week Israeli forces began a new ground offensive in central Gaza, moving tanks west of the line and issuing new forced evacuation orders.

**Context & perspectives:** Shaun Hughes, World Food Programme country director for Palestine, said that in Gaza it does not feel like a ceasefire: military control of nearly 70 percent leaves almost no space to grow food, fishing is prohibited and life-threatening, and unemployment is over 80 percent, so people have little means of survival without aid. Lilu Thapa of the Danish Refugee Council called the expanding line “displacement by design” and the ceasefire a ceasefire in name only. Ramy Abdu, founder of the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, said Israel is acquiring territory by force, and that the US-chaired Board of Peace — the body set up under the plan, with an International Stabilization Force — has no meaningful Palestinian representation and has become political cover for occupation. Mohsen Abu Ramadan of the Palestinian NGOs Network said the Board failed the international community and continues to provide political cover for atrocities. The five organisations’ scorecard is the public accounting they released as the offensive resumed.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/19/displacement-by-design-trumps-gaza-peace-plan-a-failure-aid-groups-say?traffic_source=rss) — Scorecard, Yellow Line figures, and named aid and Palestinian assessments

## Major world stories (3)

### 2) Denmark and a US security deal for Greenland
**What happened (neutral):** CNBC reported that Denmark has ratified a security deal with the Trump administration over Greenland, after months of tension in which President Donald Trump repeatedly said the United States should take control of Greenland for national security reasons. The Globe and Mail, reporting the same negotiations, said Danish lawmakers were expected to ratify the deal, and that it would expand the US military presence in Greenland, including permission to establish a Golden Dome missile-defence system.

**Context & perspectives:** The two accounts do not match on whether the vote is finished. CNBC’s report states ratification as done. The Globe and Mail still frames it as expected, and is the outlet that specifies what the text would allow: a larger American military footprint and a missile-defence site. Neither article, in the text available here, quotes a Danish minister on why parliament would accept that expansion rather than a transfer of sovereignty. What is on the page is a negotiated security arrangement set against Trump’s earlier demand for control.

**Read more (sources):**
- [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/19/greenland-denmark-trump-security-military-bases.html) — Reports ratification after Trump’s control demands
- [The Globe and Mail](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-danish-lawmakers-expected-to-ratify-trump-deal-over-greenland/) — Says ratification was expected, and names Golden Dome permission

### 3) World Court finds genocidal intent against the Rohingya
**What happened (neutral):** The International Court of Justice — the UN court that hears cases between countries — found that Myanmar acted with “genocidal intent” in specific cases during 2017 operations that, the court said, killed some 10,000 Rohingya, Al Jazeera reported. Court president Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed widespread sexual violence, used extreme violence against children, and attacked people fleeing in large numbers to Bangladesh. More than 730,000 mainly Muslim Rohingya fled in that crackdown. The Hindu’s headline on the same sitting described the ruling as ongoing even as it reported that the court found soldiers had killed and raped Rohingya, harmed children, and destroyed villages.

**Context & perspectives:** The Gambia filed the case in 2019, accusing Myanmar of trying to destroy the Rohingya and of breaching the 1948 Genocide Convention, the treaty that defines genocide and requires states to prevent and punish it. It asked the court to order an end to illegal acts against the Rohingya and punishment for those responsible. Myanmar has said the crackdown answered attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army on police posts. The New York Times noted that Aung San Suu Kyi addressed the court’s judges in 2019 and did not condemn the pogroms. The UN says more than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, with shrinking aid and dangerous sea crossings.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/19/un-top-court-finds-myanmar-killed-10000-rohingya-as-it-rules-on-genocide?traffic_source=rss) — Verdict language, death toll, and the Gambia’s 2019 case
- [The Hindu](https://www.thehindu.com/news/international/icj-verdict-on-rohingya-crackdown-killings-in-myanmar/article71719604.ece) — Court findings, with the ruling described as ongoing
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/19/world/myanmar-icj-ruling-genocide/aung-san-suu-kyi-did-not-condemn-the-pogroms-against-the-rohingya) — Suu Kyi’s 2019 appearance and her failure to condemn the pogroms

### 4) A new US–Venezuela military agreement
**CONTESTED**

**What happened (neutral):** US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a cooperation agreement with Venezuela’s interim government during an unannounced visit to Caracas on Wednesday, Al Jazeera reported. He met interim President Delcy Rodriguez and Defence Minister Gustavo Gonzalez Lopez. The two governments agreed to strengthen cooperation on joint training, intelligence sharing, military equipment and border security. Hegseth said the armed forces would work together against drug trafficking and armed groups. Rodriguez called the visit an extraordinary step and said cooperation would improve training, modernise equipment and open access to new technologies, and that it would not compromise sovereignty. Her government said the Bolivarian National Armed Forces — Venezuela’s armed forces — would benefit directly. The full terms, including how joint operations would work, have not been published.

**Context & perspectives:** The Trump administration says closer military ties will help Venezuela regain control of areas where armed groups and trafficking networks operate. The United States has, in effect, taken control of Venezuela’s oil industry since US forces abducted then-President Nicolas Maduro and took him to New York; Venezuela has the world’s largest oil reserves. On November 10 the House voted 211–204 against impeaching Hegseth for now. A resolution from Republican Thomas Massie had eight articles, covering the US–Israel war on Iran, strikes on suspected drug boats, and the January operation that removed Maduro. Massie said Hegseth ordered an act of war without congressional authorisation, and that the operation was meant to give Washington control of the oil, not only to arrest Maduro on trafficking charges. Democrats have said they want more scrutiny of the 2026 agreements with Caracas after they hold a House majority.

**The disagreement:** Everything turns on a text the public has not seen. Hegseth and Rodriguez present the agreement as a practical security tool: shared training, intelligence, equipment and border work against traffickers and armed groups, with Rodriguez adding that Venezuela’s forces get modern kit without giving up sovereignty. Political analyst Carlos Pina locates the visit in US politics after the November 3 midterms, when Democrats said they would scrutinise Venezuela policy, and after the failed impeachment push — a trip, in his reading, to get ahead of the next Congress. Massie’s articles supply the sharper charge about the earlier operation: that it was war for oil reserves, not a drug arrest. His own text concedes the narrow vote already failed, 211–204, and the new agreement’s operational clauses are still unpublished, so neither the sovereignty promise nor the oil motive can be checked against the document.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/19/why-is-pete-hegseth-strengthening-us-military-ties-with-venezuela?traffic_source=rss) — Deal areas, Caracas meetings, Pina, and the impeachment vote

## Economy, science & technology (2)

### 5) An energy-security path that could cut oil use
**What happened (neutral):** A response built around energy security after the war in Iran could cut oil demand by 4 percent by 2035, the International Energy Agency said, Reuters reported. The New York Times, on the same analysis, said it was the agency’s most comprehensive look at the war’s fallout, and that the oil shock could speed adoption of other power sources.

**Context & perspectives:** The figure is a scenario for global oil demand a decade out, not a measure of this month’s barrels. The Times ties that path to a faster shift toward power that is not oil. Neither dispatch, in the text available here, lists which countries’ policies produce the 4 percent.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/energy-security-response-iran-war-could-cut-oil-demand-by-4-by-2035-iea-says-2026-11-19/) — The 4 percent by 2035 figure
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/business/cop31-energy-iea.html) — Oil shock and faster adoption of other power sources

### 6) Iran’s blockade, and two readings of whether it works

**What happened (neutral):** Iran’s economy is expected to shrink further under a US naval blockade of its ports, overland trade disruptions and sanctions, Al Jazeera reported, with the pain falling on tens of millions of people. Official figures show gross domestic product shrank 10.1 percent year on year between March 21 and June 20, the first quarter of the Persian calendar. Tehran-based economist Peyman Molavi said that if conditions hold, money-supply growth could rise from nearly 51 percent to 55–60 percent by late March, and that annual inflation could reach about 85 percent, with point-to-point inflation at 100 percent, hitting energy, food, metals and industrial goods hardest. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the embargo will produce a 25 percent contraction by the year ending March 2027. Central bank governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said the bank has secured 30 billion dollars in foreign currency for the coming months, with essential goods first. Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said all overland routes remain open except one with Iraq, closed for security reasons. Al Jazeera also reported that the US has brought a third aircraft carrier into the region to support a possible escalation. AP reported separately that the US military is back to two aircraft carriers in the Middle East. Those two counts are not the same, and neither dispatch here reconciles them.

**Context & perspectives:** After a deadlock in the US–Israel war on Iran, which began with strikes that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on February 28, Washington has demanded that Tehran reopen the Strait of Hormuz and curb its nuclear programme. Iranian authorities say they can withstand the pressure and have set out their own demands. For decades governments in Tehran have covered budget deficits by printing money, which has fed chronic inflation; the currency crunch from disrupted oil exports has made that worse.

**The disagreement:** The shared ground is a shrinking economy: a 10.1 percent drop in that first quarter, and a blockade both governments treat as real. Bessent’s case is that the embargo is doing the work he wants — a 25 percent contraction by March 2027, large enough to force a political result. Hemmati’s reply is that it is too early to count the winter, and that 30 billion dollars is already set aside so essential imports continue. Madanizadeh adds a mechanism: neighbours’ land routes, except the Iraq crossing, are still open, so isolation is not total. Hemmati does not claim the pressure is painless; his argument is that reserves and time keep a collapse, or a forced concession, from being a result already in hand.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/11/19/too-early-to-determine-impact-of-us-siege-on-iran-with-tehran-defiant?traffic_source=rss) — GDP, inflation estimates, Bessent, Hemmati, and a third carrier
- [AP News](https://apnews.com/article/iran-war-aircraft-carrier-uss-george-washington-f72d5aa085500412989183e606bfadfd) — US military back to two carriers in the region

## Progress watch (1)

### 7) UniCredit and Berlin clear a path on Commerzbank
**What happened (neutral):** Italy’s UniCredit struck a deal with Germany that clears a path for a takeover of Commerzbank, The Wall Street Journal reported. UniCredit agreed to keep Commerzbank’s headquarters in Frankfurt, where the bank will remain listed, and Germany will no longer seek to nominate members directly to Commerzbank’s board. The complication is built into that trade: Berlin gives up a direct hand on the board so a foreign bank can proceed, while the headquarters and the listing stay in Frankfurt.

**Context & perspectives:** The article does not state a purchase price or a closing date. What it records is a completed political bargain on place and board seats, not a finished merger.

**Read more (sources):**
- [The Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/business/unicredit-strikes-deal-with-germany-to-clear-path-for-commerzbank-takeover-8668f619?mod=rss_worldnews) — Headquarters, listing, and an end to direct German board nominations

### Also Today
**South Korea court orders retrial of ex-PM Han in 2024 martial law case: South China Morning Post**
South Korea’s top court overturned former prime minister Han Duck-soo’s 15-year sentence for aiding the December 2024 martial-law declaration and sent the case back to a lower court; the decree, issued by then-president Yoon Suk-yeol, lasted about six hours. Source: [scmp.com](https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/east-asia/article/3375086/south-korea-court-orders-retrial-ex-pm-han-2024-martial-law-case)

**Netanyahu Associates Acknowledge Role in Setting Off Election Day Arrests: The New York Times**
After a historic result for Israel’s Arab-led parties, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the vote was rigged, pointing to the detention of three opposition activists, and his chief of staff has admitted a role in the first outreach to police. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/world/middleeast/netanyahu-arab-activists-arrests-israel-election.html)

**Crimea bridge has been attacked again, says Russian-installed governor: The Guardian**
Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, said the remaining Kerch rail bridge was attacked overnight and that trains would start crossing from about 4 p.m. Thursday, two days after a Ukrainian raid knocked out the road section. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/19/kerch-bridge-crimea-russia-attacked-again-ukraine)

**Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi missiles targeting Riyadh and south: Al Jazeera**
The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a Houthi missile toward Riyadh, with material damage from debris still being measured, and later destroyed four ballistic missiles fired toward the south. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/19/saudi-led-coalition-intercepts-houthi-missiles-targeting-riyadh-and-south?traffic_source=rss)

**Uncontacted Awá of Brazil Emerge From Rainforest Seeking Food: The New York Times**
A group of 20 people came out of the forest and asked for food, an Indigenous peoples’ rights group said, raising fears that environmental damage left them no choice. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/world/americas/brazil-amazon-indigenous-contact.html)

**Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut: BBC**
The BBC reported that Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, raised 81 billion dollars in its stock-market debut, while NPR reported a raise of more than 100 billion dollars, with shares due to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday. Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6742m39xgzxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Data center electricity use could double by 2030, IEA says: CNBC**
The International Energy Agency said global electricity use by data centres could double by 2030 as the AI boom adds pressure to power grids. Source: [cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/19/data-center-electricity-demand-iea.html)

**Infantino to face France's Diallo and Japan's Tashima in FIFA presidential election: France24**
FIFA confirmed that Philippe Diallo of France and Kozo Tashima of Japan will run against Gianni Infantino in next year’s presidential election. Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/sport/20261119-infantino-to-face-france-s-diallo-and-japan-s-tashima-in-fifa-presidential-election)

**Japanese PM Takaichi calls for continued dialogue with China to ease bilateral tensions: The Hindu**
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called for continued dialogue with China to ease tensions, after shaking hands with President Xi Jinping and meeting President Vladimir Putin the same day. Source: [thehindu.com](https://www.thehindu.com/news/international/japanese-pm-takaichi-calls-for-continued-dialogue-with-china-to-ease-bilateral-tensions/article71719391.ece)

**Yunus's ancestral home set ablaze as violence grips Bangladesh: The Hindu**
Muhammad Yunus’s ancestral home was set ablaze, and newspaper reports said rival activists, presumed to be from Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Bangladesh Nationalist Party, attacked or burned homes of two Awami League leaders in Dhaka overnight. Source: [thehindu.com](https://www.thehindu.com/news/international/yunuss-ancestral-home-set-ablaze-as-violence-grips-bangladesh/article71719029.ece)

**Trump makes third Supreme Court bid to end Venezuelan migrant protections: Al Jazeera**
President Trump made a third emergency appeal to the US Supreme Court to end temporary protected status for Venezuelan migrants, after a California judge ruled that ending it was unlawful. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/19/trump-makes-third-supreme-court-bid-to-end-venezuelan-migrant-protections?traffic_source=rss)

**Supreme Court urged to defang ‘criminal trap’ that has sent Trump officials to prison: Fox News**
Peter Navarro asked the Supreme Court to overturn his contempt-of-Congress convictions, arguing that a willfulness requirement would make such prosecutions harder to prove. Source: [foxnews.com](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/supreme-court-urged-defang-criminal-trap-sent-trump-officials-prison)

**Trump's historic summit with Xi, Putin marks diplomatic milestone, but breakthroughs remain elusive: Fox News**
President Trump, President Xi Jinping and President Vladimir Putin held three-way talks in Shenzhen for more than an hour on nuclear arms cuts and the war in Ukraine, and no major breakthrough was announced. Source: [foxnews.com](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/trumps-historic-summit-xi-putin-marks-diplomatic-milestone-breakthroughs-remain-elusive)

**Tusk appears to mock Trump’s Putin comment as Ukraine’s allies meet in Berlin: The Guardian**
After the US president called Putin a friend, Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk said, “God, protect us from such friends.” Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/nov/19/russia-ukraine-war-coalition-of-the-willing-europe-latest-news-updates)

## Understanding the Issue: Why an oil customer is not a political guarantor
A common misreading is that a willing buyer in China makes an economic blockade of Iran fail, or succeed, as a unit. Deutsche Welle reports that in 2025 Chinese buyers took more than 80 percent of Iran’s seaborne crude, much of it through independent refiners and at a steep discount because of sanctions, while Iran grew more dependent on Chinese machinery, electronics and industrial inputs. Mohsen Solhdoost, an assistant professor of international relations at Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, told Deutsche Welle that if the aim is to cut export earnings, restrict equipment and slow economic and military recovery, the United States can get substantial results without Chinese cooperation — and that interrupting trade is easier to show than determining another government’s political choices. In November, Washington announced Task Force Iron Gate, aimed at disrupting sanctioned goods, military equipment and revenue across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea; goods still move through countries including Iraq, Pakistan and Turkey, under greater scrutiny. Solhdoost’s point is physical: a Chinese buyer cannot keep export revenue flowing by staying willing to buy if newly loaded tankers cannot reach the market. A senior official at Iran’s Plan and Budget Organization said the government was preparing its 2027–2028 budget under several scenarios, including oil revenue at zero — not a decision to adopt that budget, but a sign Tehran is planning for the lifeline to fail. Rail and road can still move spare parts and keep selected factories running; they cannot replace ships at the same scale or cost. Beijing’s economic tie, Solhdoost says, does not mean support for every Iranian policy, and both China and Russia weigh Tehran against their own dealings with Washington. Reading a blockade story, the check is simple: separate what a buyer was willing to purchase from what actually sailed, and see whether the budget on the table still assumes oil income. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/iran-balances-ties-with-china-and-russia-as-trump-ramps-up-pressure/a-79979920?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

## Media-literacy note
When two wire services give different counts for the same deployment, or one desk says a vote is finished and another says it is still expected, the honest move is to name both and wait for the document. A court reading, a scorecard and a budget scenario are all checkable against the institution that issued them. Pick one story from today and open the primary text — a judgment, a treaty note, or the agency release — beside a second newsroom that does not share the first one’s habits.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **Democrats hold fifty-six Senate seats after Mary Peltola wins Alaska.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) Mary Peltola wins Alaska’s Senate seat — CONTESTED
**What happened (neutral):** Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska’s United States Senate seat, unseating two-term Republican Dan Sullivan, Al Jazeera reports, with The Associated Press count at 50.1 percent of first-choice votes to Sullivan’s 45.8 percent and an estimated 99 percent of votes counted. The British Broadcasting Corporation, or BBC, reports that confirmation of her victory caps the Democrats’ rout of Republicans in the midterm Senate election. Al Jazeera reports her win gives Democrats 56 seats to the Republicans’ 44, and that it is the Democrats’ first Senate win in Alaska in more than a decade. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, so a candidate with a majority of first-choice votes is elected outright, with no further rounds. Peltola, a Yup’ik Alaskan, was the first Alaska Native elected to Congress when she won a special election for the state’s only House seat in 2022; she served until January 2025 and lost re-election in 2024.

**Context & perspectives:** A second candidate, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan, appeared on the ballot with no party affiliation beside incumbent “Dan S Sullivan.” The state elections division removed the retired teacher in June, saying he had chosen the name to cause confusion and pointing to a consultant who had previously worked for Peltola; a superior court judge ruled him eligible, and the Alaska Supreme Court upheld that on June 29. The Trump administration alleged that Peltola’s campaign had deliberately recruited the second Sullivan to divide Republican votes, a practice called ballot stacking. Al Jazeera reports that even if the incumbent had received every vote cast for his namesake, he still would not have beaten Peltola. Scott Lucas, a professor at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute, told Al Jazeera that Peltola is viewed as a pragmatist who played down the Democratic label and stressed energy jobs, border security and gun rights, and that Sullivan was hurt by being tied to President Donald Trump’s ticket.

The Trump administration’s case is that a near-identical name was put on the ballot to split Republican votes, and that a consultant linked to Peltola’s earlier campaign is evidence the second Sullivan was not an ordinary independent. The count and the courts cut the other way: judges kept Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot as eligible, and the Associated Press tally, as reported by Al Jazeera, shows the namesake votes were not large enough to change the winner.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/18/why-democrat-mary-peltolas-us-senate-win-in-alaska-matters?traffic_source=rss) — vote shares, ranked-choice rule, ballot fight, and Senate arithmetic
- [BBC](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqev3v2ygzlvo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss) — confirmation that the Alaska result caps the Democrats’ Senate rout

## Major world stories (3)
### 1) Trump arrives in Shenzhen as allies split on Ukraine’s deep strikes — CONTESTED
**What happened (neutral):** After a stop in Manila, President Donald Trump has landed in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, or APEC, summit, CNBC reports, ahead of talks on Thursday with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. National Public Radio, or NPR, reports that Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac, returning a gesture Trump made when Xi visited Washington in September. CNBC reports that the three-way meeting is expected to focus on the Iran war, Russia’s war in Ukraine and strategic stability, and that expectations of a concrete outcome are low. A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said Monday that the three were expected to hold in-depth talks on peace and strategic stability. Xi opened the summit calling for free trade, cooperation on artificial intelligence and a green transition, saying, “We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition.” Putin told the summit that sanctions on Russia have backfired. The Guardian’s live coverage reports that Putin described Europe as being in “humiliating decline.”

**Context & perspectives:** Xi met Putin earlier Wednesday, before Trump arrived; Chinese state media said Xi called for a more stable business environment and a “multipolar world,” while Putin spoke of expanding trade, energy and education, and those reports did not address Ukraine or Iran. Xi also met South Korea’s Lee Jae Myung; Seoul’s readout said they discussed peace on the Korean Peninsula, which Beijing’s record omitted. Trump is also due to meet Xi bilaterally, with hopes of a trade truce beyond January 2027, as the United States seeks to curb exports of artificial intelligence chips. The New York Times reports that U.S. intelligence says Putin will continue the Ukraine war despite the planned meeting, and that Trump has halted some sanctions on Russia and announced that the United States will buy Russian diesel.

Ahead of those talks, Germany and the United Kingdom rejected U.S. criticism of Ukraine’s deep strikes inside Russia, CNBC reports. At the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or NATO, headquarters on Tuesday, U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby said those deep strikes have not driven an end to the war or blunted Russia’s front-line advances, and that strikes he called hits on civilian infrastructure — citing retailer Wildberries — have probably hardened Russian public resolve. He also said Ukraine’s mid-range drone campaign has been “very effective,” and that Ukraine’s forces gained more territory than Russia in October for a second straight month. Kyiv says warehouses it hit supplied Russian forces with drone parts and navigation gear; Wildberries and the Kremlin deny the firm is involved in the war. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said criticizing strikes meant to destroy strategic military and military-use targets “is quite a stupid thing, I think,” and that criticism should instead fall on what he called nightly “terroristic” Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy, water and heating. British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said it is “not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war,” and that the strikes have degraded Putin’s war machine, “buying time and saving lives.”

Colby’s argument is that spectacle far behind the front does not stop Russian advances and can make the Kremlin more willing to escalate, while the campaign that actually matters is the one denying ground at the front — a limit he himself marks by calling that mid-range effort effective. Pistorius and Streeting answer that Ukraine is hitting military-use targets, that outsiders should not dictate Kyiv’s tactics, and that the strikes raise Moscow’s costs; they do not claim, in these remarks, that deep strikes alone will end the war.

**Questions to consider:** By the close of Thursday’s Shenzhen talks, is there any joint line from Trump, Xi and Putin on Ukraine’s strikes inside Russia, or only separate statements?

**Read more (sources):**
- [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/18/trump-xi-putin-china-apec.html) — arrival, summit agenda and leaders’ opening remarks
- [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/18/nx-s1-6045518/trump-china-xi-putin) — Xi’s tarmac greeting
- [AP](https://apnews.com/article/apec-china-economy-trump-putin-ai-1e3b6161b31196c9716ca02ac8c7720c) — Xi on open trade and Putin on sanctions
- [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/nov/18/apec-summit-live-updates-xi-putin-trump-world-leaders-gather-in-china) — Putin’s remark on Europe
- [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/18/ukraine-russia-war-trump-putin-deep-strikes.html) — U.S., German and British clash over deep strikes
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/us/politics/trump-putin-ukraine-war.html) — intelligence assessment, sanctions pause and Russian diesel

### 2) European Commission proposes a €45 billion Ukraine loan
**What happened (neutral):** European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed a €45 billion loan to Ukraine for 2027, France24 reports, to help cover around two-thirds of Kyiv’s financing needs. She said the loan would be repaid through future war reparations by Russia.

**Context & perspectives:** The Commission is the European Union’s executive body. The announcement is a proposal: France24 does not report that member governments have approved it, or name a date for that decision. No opposing government is quoted in the report.

**Read more (sources):**
- [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261118-eu-proposes-new-%E2%82%AC45-billion-ukraine-loan-to-be-repaid-by-russia) — size of the proposed 2027 loan and the repayment claim

### 3) Haitians march for El Salvador’s troops in Port-au-Prince
**What happened (neutral):** Thousands of Haitians marched in Port-au-Prince on Tuesday in support of soldiers from El Salvador sent by President Nayib Bukele against armed gangs, Al Jazeera reports, with signs reading “Thank you, Bukele” and “Long live Bukele.” Bukele has sent more than 2,000 troops since late October, after four Salvadoran soldiers went missing during an operation by the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force. That latest deployment is separate from the force, and Haitian authorities have welcomed it. On November 10, Bukele said he had destroyed the “headquarters” of one of Haiti’s main gangs and released video of a helicopter attack. Salvadoran forces, backed by Haiti’s national police, have since taken control of a football stadium in the capital.

**Context & perspectives:** Bukele’s gang crackdown at home has broad public support and has drawn accusations of human rights violations; the report does not name the accusers. On Tuesday the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights urged all security forces in Haiti to protect civilians and to use lethal force only as a last resort. In the first 10 months of this year, the United Nations recorded 4,595 killings and 2,050 injuries linked to armed violence in Haiti.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/11/18/photos-thousands-march-in-haiti-in-support-of-salvadoran-troops?traffic_source=rss) — the march, troop numbers, stadium, and United Nations casualty figures

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 1) UK inflation rises to 3.6 percent
**What happened (neutral):** United Kingdom inflation rose to a 12-month high of 3.6 percent in October, up from 3.5 percent in September, the South China Morning Post reports, citing the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday. Petrol and diesel costs and tobacco duty changes pushed the Consumer Prices Index up. The reading matched economists’ predictions and was the fourth monthly increase in a row, moving inflation further from the Bank of England’s target. The report does not state the target figure.

**Context & perspectives:** The Office for National Statistics is the United Kingdom’s official statistics agency. The Bank of England is the central bank that sets interest rates with an inflation target in mind. No official is quoted on what the bank will do next.

**Read more (sources):**
- [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/news/world/europe/article/3374912/uk-inflation-hits-12-month-high-36-soaring-fuel-tobacco-costs) — October CPI, the September comparison, and the fuel and tobacco drivers

### 2) Arsenic from Myanmar mining shuts taps in northern Thailand
**What happened (neutral):** Thai authorities have rushed clean water to more than 20,000 households in Chiang Rai after unsafe arsenic, linked to mining in Myanmar, was found in the supply, Al Jazeera reports. Tap water to thousands of homes in 14 villages in Mae Sai district, near the Myanmar border, was suspended this month after arsenic in the local waterworks tested at 30 times the safe limit. Untreated water from the Sai River, a Mekong tributary, was at 25 times the drinking-water limit. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul late on Tuesday ordered agencies to find other sources and to watch tap quality, deputy government spokeswoman Lalida Persvivatana said. Two trucks are supplying drinking water, and the government is considering other rivers.

**Context & perspectives:** Researchers at Naresuan University said last week that chemical analysis and satellite modelling traced much of the arsenic-laden sediment in the Sai River to gold mining across the border in Myanmar. A surge in rare earth mining in rebel-held parts of Myanmar that supply Chinese processing plants is being blamed for heavy metals in Thai waterways, including the Mekong; Myanmar’s civil war enables unregulated digging of elements used in phones, wind turbines and electric vehicles. Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, visiting Myanmar last week, called a “dramatic” rise in Sai River pollution from mining wastewater urgent. The Thai government says it has also raised the issue with Beijing; researchers say many of the Myanmar mines are Chinese-run. Officials said arsenic was found in the urine of 17 of 177 people tested in October in Nong Khai, on the Laos border.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/18/arsenic-pollution-linked-to-myanmar-mining-prompts-water-alert-in-thailand?traffic_source=rss) — test multiples, the university tracing, and the emergency water response

## Progress watch (1)
### 1) Rio Tinto agrees to pay $250 million over a closed Papua New Guinea mine
**What happened (neutral):** Rio Tinto will pay $250 million to address environmental damage from its long-closed mine in Papua New Guinea, The New York Times reports, in a deal the paper calls a landmark. The money will also go toward remedying human rights problems caused by that mine.

**Context & perspectives:** The complication is built into the payment: the mine is already long closed, so the sum is for harm already done, not for an operating site. The Times report, as provided, does not compare the sum with an earlier offer or with an estimate of total damage.

**Read more (sources):**
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/world/asia/rio-tinto-papua-new-guinea-mine.html) — the $250 million remedy payment

### Also Today
**Former Malaysian minister calls on Indonesia to pay US$3 billion for haze losses: South China Morning Post**
Former finance minister Lim Guan Eng called on Indonesia to pay losses he put at 13 billion ringgit, about 3 billion U.S. dollars, from this year’s haze, or to form a permanent task force, while also saying Malaysia should accept President Prabowo Subianto’s apology. **Iran widens Gulf attacks, firing on a US air base in Kuwait and at targets in Bahrain: AP News**
Iran widened Gulf attacks by firing on a United States air base in Kuwait and at targets in Bahrain, the Associated Press reports. Source: [apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/iran-us-kuwait-gulf-attacks-bahrain-b1f0b530cffe951e6fcc1e27b2e1af94)

**Ethiopia: El Niño, Iran War Shocks Could Push Nearly One Million More Ethiopians Into Poverty: AllAfrica**
The International Food Policy Research Institute warns that a strong El Niño plus higher fuel prices linked to the Iran war could push nearly 905,000 more Ethiopians into poverty and 2.8 million into undernourishment in 2027. Source: [allafrica.com](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611180198.html)

**Italy approves antisemitism law amid leftist opposition protests: Reuters**

**U.S. Energy Chief Urges Western Europe to Pivot to Power Expansion: WSJ**
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Western Europe has done too little to grow its energy supply and needs an “energy-addition” approach. Source: [wsj.com](https://www.wsj.com/world/europe/u-s-energy-chief-urges-western-europe-to-pivot-to-power-expansion-e75d8bfe?mod=rss_worldnews)

**Carney says Canada’s growing trade ties with China are not a top concern for Trump: AP News**
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada’s growing trade ties with China are not a top concern for President Trump. Source: [apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/apec-canada-carney-trump-xi-0a52cf279d85c6ddd69b985d742f148d)

## Understanding the Issue: How an economy can grow while burning less fuel
A common misreading is that a growing economy must burn more coal, oil and gas, so any rise in fuel prices is treated as proof that climate policy and growth cannot share a year. Deutsche Welle reports that Earth has already crossed seven of the nine planetary boundaries scientists treat as critical for life, including climate change, ocean acidification and biosphere integrity. Green growth, as social ecologist Helmut Haberl of BOKU University in Vienna describes it, means “business as usual, but with more sustainable technologies”: wind and solar instead of coal and gas, heat pumps instead of gas furnaces, and more reuse of materials. Haberl and colleagues published a 2020 report weighing more than 800 studies. Scenarios from the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change show economic output can keep rising while emissions from coal, oil and gas fall sharply, and Deutsche Welle reports that this has already happened for years in the United Kingdom, the United States, Japan and Australia, even when offshore production is counted. In the European Union, the economy has grown by more than 70 percent since 1990 while carbon emissions have dropped by around 40 percent — a full split Haberl’s group still calls relatively rare. In India and in several countries in Africa and Southeast Asia, production is getting cleaner per unit, but emissions are still rising, which does not match the path needed to avoid the worst climate damage. Steel and chemicals are harder still, because carbon is part of the process, not only the fuel, and substitutes such as green hydrogen need heavy investment. A further catch, the rebound effect, is that cheaper green production can lead firms and households to use more, eating part of the savings. Reading a fuel-price story with that map means separating a month’s petrol bill from the longer emissions trend, and not treating one country’s decoupling as a global result. The next time a government boasts of green growth, check whether the emissions number includes offshore production, and whether total resource use fell or only the fuel burned per product. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/how-a-green-economy-could-help-reverse-climate-change/a-79874576?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

## Media-literacy note
When two outlets cover the same result, read the one that shows the count beside the one that only confirms the winner. A proposal is not a law, and a minister’s call for payment is not a signed transfer. Primary documents — a court ruling, a statistics release, a treaty text — still beat a live blog’s mood.

**Go deeper:** Al Jazeera reports Peltola’s 50.1 percent to Sullivan’s 45.8 percent and the fight over a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot; the BBC confirms the win as the cap on the Democrats’ Senate rout without those shares or that ballot dispute.
